docs.text: genanki2 Generate, read and update Anki decks using Python. genanki2 reads and writes .apkg / .colpkg packages using Anki's latest collection schema (v18). It is a spiritual successor to genanki , which has been unmaintained for a few years and uses the old v11 schema. Coming from genanki? See Migrating from genanki . Highlights: ⭐ Generate packages: simple-to-use API, inspired by genanki, while fixing many of its issues. ⭐ Read packages: inspect, update and fix your packages. Extract media files to disk for easy management. ⭐ No more hardcoded ids: build a package once , genanki2 generates unique ids for you. Then read, update and write again a new version: ids and guids come back out of the file, so your script doesn't have to hardcode them anymore. The next import updates the decks that users already have instead of adding a duplicate. ⭐ Comprehensive checks and repairs: genanki2 refuses to write what Anki would reject or change on import and warns about possible mistakes. Installation pip install genanki2 # or uv add genanki2 genanki2 needs Python 3.10 or newer. No Anki install required! Quick start Build a deck and write it: from genanki2 import deck, guid_for, note, notetype, package # The package holds the media files, the collection holds everything else pkg, collection = package() # A notetype: its fields, and a (name, front, back) template per card type word = notetype( name="Italian word", fields=["Italian", "English", "Audio"], templates=[ ("Recognition", "{{Italian}}", "{{FrontSide}}<hr id=answer>{{English}}"), ("Recall", "{{English}}", "{{FrontSide}}<hr id=answer>{{Italian}}"), ("Listening", "{{Audio}}", "{{FrontSide}}<hr id=answer>{{Italian}}"), ], id=1_759_600_000_000, # a fixed id, so a rebuild updates the notetype ) # guid_for() derives a note's guid from a key that stays the same on every build notes = [ note(word, ["casa", "house", ""], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")), note(word, ["cane", "dog", ""], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "cane")), ] # "::" makes a subdeck vocabulary = deck("Italian::Vocabulary") # Two cards per note: "Listening" is skipped because "Audio" is empty collection.add_notes(notes, vocabulary) pkg.write_apkg("italian.apkg") Open italian.apkg with File > Import in Anki. Later, update the deck by reading the package back: from genanki2 import Package, guid_for, note pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) collection = pkg.collection # Find objects by name or identifier word = collection.get_notetype(name="Italian word") casa = collection.get_note(guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")) vocabulary = collection.get_deck(name="Italian::Vocabulary") # Set fields by name casa["English"] = "house, home" # Update notes with new media files and generate missing cards pkg.media.append("audio/it_casa.mp3") casa["Audio"] = "[sound:it_casa.mp3]" collection.generate_missing_cards() # Adds the missing "Listening" card # Add new notes finestra = note(word, ["finestra", "window", ""], guid=guid_for(word.id, "finestra")) collection.add_notes([finestra], vocabulary) pkg.write_apkg("italian-v2.apkg") Anyone who imports italian-v2.apkg over the first version gets the corrected note and three new cards, and keeps the schedule of the cards they were already studying. docs.text: Migrating from genanki genanki writes packages using an old collection format (schema v11). genanki2 writes the latest collection format (schema v18) and it can also read packages. Migration from genanki to genanki2 depends on whether you have the package build script or not. If you do, simply translate it: see Translating a build script . It is recommended to use stable ids so that you can rerun the build script. See Identifiers that keep a deck updatable . If you don't have a build script, but you have a shared package ( .apkg file), try to use genanki2 to read it. If the package was written directly by genanki, the read will fail, telling you that genanki2 cannot read a v11 package. You will need to re-export a genanki-written deck using Anki. From then on, use a read-update-write flow with genanki2 to maintain your package. Re-export a genanki-written deck Import the package into Anki and export it again: In Anki, choose File > Export. Pick Anki Deck Package and your deck. Tick Include media . Untick Include scheduling information , so that your own review history does not ship with the deck. Untick Support older Anki versions . Read the export with Package.read_apkg(path, keep_source_media=True) , then change it and write a new version as described in Updating a package . Reimporting the updated package does not create duplicates in your collection (apart as consequences of your updates) because the package contains all the identifiers that genanki wrote. See Identifiers that keep a deck updatable for details. Finding notes genanki2.guid_for() hashes differently from genanki.guid_for() , so if your update script uses this pattern, it will fail: # The original build script: import genanki word = genanki.Model(1607392319, "Italian word", fields=[...], templates=[...]) casa = genanki.Note( model=word, fields=["casa", "house"], guid=genanki.guid_for(word.model_id, "casa") ) print(casa.guid) # MM8Z-D@is/ deck = genanki.Deck(2059400110, "Italian") deck.add_note(casa) genanki.Package(deck).write_to_file("italian.apkg") # Import italian.apkg into Anki and export it again # The genanki2 update script: from genanki2 import Package, guid_for pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) word = pkg.collection.get_notetype(name="Italian word") print(word.id) # 1607392319 print(guid_for(word.id, "casa")) # BMv|*`)wXK print(pkg.collection.get_note(guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa"))) # None Solutions: Find by fields. Build a dictionary from fields that identify the note, as examples/read_update_write.py does with {note["Italian"]: note for note in collection.notes} . Find by genanki's guid. If your script called genanki.guid_for(*key) with stable values, compute the same guid and look it up with collection.get_note(guid=...) . Here is a recipe: import hashlib BASE91 = ( "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789" "!#$%&()*+,-./:;<=>?@[]^_`{|}~" ) def genanki_guid_for(*values: object) -> str: digest = hashlib.sha256("__".join(str(v) for v in values).encode()).digest() n = int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big") out = "" while n > 0: n, r = divmod(n, len(BASE91)) out = BASE91[r] + out return out Then later you can use pkg.collection.get_note(guid=genanki_guid_for(word.id, "casa")) . genanki's unstable default: A note built without guid= got genanki's default guid, a hash of all its field values, which changes when a field's value changes. Find those notes by a stable set of fields (solution 1). Field and template ids genanki writes fields and templates without ids, so Anki matches them by name, and renaming one makes the next import add a second notetype. Call Notetype.fill_missing_ids() on each notetype in the first version you ship with genanki2. The import gives the user's notetype those ids, and from then on a rename is matched by id. See Changing a notetype's fields or templates . Translating a build script The overall shape stays the same: notetypes, notes, a deck, a package. Step genanki genanki2 Start pkg, col = package() Notetype m = Model(1607392319, "Simple", fields=[...], templates=[...]) m = notetype("Simple", ["Q", "A"], [("Card 1", qfmt, afmt)], id=1607392319) Note n = Note(model=m, fields=["q", "a"]) n = note(m, ["q", "a"]) Deck d = Deck(2059400110, "Capitals") d = deck("Capitals") Add d.add_note(n) col.add_notes([n], d) Write Package(d).write_to_file("out.apkg") pkg.write_apkg("out.apkg") package() returns two objects. The package holds the media and is read from and written to disk; the collection holds the decks, notetypes and notes. Notes belong to the collection, and each card points at its deck. col.add_notes() reads the whole collection on every call, so add all the notes for a deck in one call rather than one call per note. Notetypes genanki genanki2 Model(model_id, name, ...) notetype(name, ..., id=model_id) fields=[{"name": "Q"}] ["Q"] fields=[{"name": "Q", "font": "Arial", "size": 20}] [field("Q", font_name="Arial", font_size=20)] templates=[{"name": n, "qfmt": q, "afmt": a}] [(n, q, a)] or [template(n, q, a)] css=... , latex_pre=... , latex_post=... the same keyword arguments on notetype() sort_field_index=1 sort_field="A" or sort_field_idx=1 model_type=Model.CLOZE cloze=True m.set_fields(...) , m.set_templates(...) m.fields = [...] , m.templates = [...] The other keys of a field or template dictionary become keyword arguments of field() and template() : genanki key genanki2 keyword font , size font_name , font_size rtl , sticky right_to_left , sticky bqfmt , bafmt q_format_browser , a_format_browser bfont , bsize browser_font_name , browser_font_size did target_deck_id media none, Anki no longer stores it genanki also accepts fields and templates as a YAML string. genanki2 takes Python lists only. Without id , notetype() makes up a new id each run, and every rebuild then arrives as a new notetype. Pass a fixed id (see Identifiers that keep a deck updatable ), or read the notetype from the previous package. genanki works out a note's cards by approximating Anki's rules and the approximation is wrong for some templates. genanki2 applies Anki's rules (see Card generation ), so a note can get more or fewer cards than genanki wrote. genanki's errors: Note genanki genanki2 and Anki front {{#A}}{{B}}{{/A}}{{C}} , only A filled no card card 0, through the fallback front {{text:A}} , A filled no card card 0 a field holding only a space counted as filled counted as empty a cloze in a field the template does not pass through cloze: ignored gives a card {{c1,2::…}} card 0 cards 0 and 1 {{c1::{{c2::…}}}} card 0 cards 0 and 1 {{c600::…}} card 599 card 499 genanki writes a note without any card when its requirements fail, where Anki would give it card 0. Notes genanki genanki2 Note(model=m, fields=[...]) note(m, [...]) tags=["a", "b"] tags=["a", "b"] guid=... guid=... guid_for(*values) guid_for(notetype_id, *key) , which gives other guids sort_field=... none, Anki computes it from the notetype's sort field due=5 card.due = 5 on the cards col.add_notes() returns n.cards[1].suspend = True cards[1].suspend() , on the cards col.add_notes() returns n.fields[0] n.fields[0] , or n["Q"] by field name Without guid , genanki hashes all the field values, so editing a field turns the note into a new one on the user's side. genanki2 picks a random guid instead, which is not better for a rebuild: pass a guid (see Identifiers that keep a deck updatable ), or read the note from the previous package. genanki2.guid_for() gives other guids than genanki.guid_for() for the same values. For a deck people have already imported, keep genanki's guids: use genanki_guid_for() from Finding notes and call it where the script called genanki.guid_for() . genanki gives every card position 0. genanki2 numbers new cards in the order that notes are added, which is the order they are studied in. A tag cannot contain a space. genanki2 also cleans each part of a tag (separated by :: ) the way Anki does. col.add_notes() returns the cards grouped per note, in the order of the notes: for front, back in col.add_notes(notes, d): back.suspend() A suspension reaches the user only when they tick "Import any learning progress" while importing. Without it, which is the default, Anki imports every card as a new card and keeps only its position. Decks genanki genanki2 Deck(deck_id, name) deck(name) description="..." description="..." d.add_note(n) col.add_notes([n], d) d.add_model(m) not needed, the notes bring their notetype d.write_to_file(path) pkg.write_apkg(path) Anki recognises a deck by its name, so genanki2 has no deck id to keep stable. An import creates only the decks and notetypes that the package's cards use. An empty deck is not imported by Anki. Packages and media genanki genanki2 Package([d1, d2]) one pkg, col = package() , with every deck in col Package(d, media_files=["a.mp3"]) pkg.media.append("a.mp3") p.write_to_file(path) pkg.write_apkg(path) genanki packs media in no fixed order, and two paths with the same file name both get packed under that one name. genanki2 keeps the order you append in and refuses two paths with the same file name. pkg.trim_unused_media() drops every media file that no note, template or stylesheet refers to. Builtin notetypes genanki genanki2 BASIC_MODEL BASIC_NOTETYPE BASIC_AND_REVERSED_CARD_MODEL BASIC_AND_REVERSED_NOTETYPE BASIC_OPTIONAL_REVERSED_CARD_MODEL BASIC_OPTIONAL_REVERSED_NOTETYPE BASIC_TYPE_IN_THE_ANSWER_MODEL BASIC_TYPE_IN_THE_ANSWER_NOTETYPE CLOZE_MODEL CLOZE_NOTETYPE IMAGE_OCCLUSION_NOTETYPE These have different ids from genanki's, so to Anki they are different notetypes. A deck that used BASIC_MODEL and is rebuilt with BASIC_NOTETYPE gives its users a second notetype and a second copy of every note. For a deck people have already imported, read the notetype from the export instead, as described in Re-export a genanki-written deck . What genanki2 does not have write_to_file(path, timestamp=...) , which genanki uses to make ids and modification times repeatable between runs. write_to_collection_from_addon() and write_to_db() , which write into an open Anki collection from an add-on.

Building a deck Building and writing a package 1. Create a package holding a collection API Models from genanki2 import package pkg, collection = package() from genanki2 import Collection, Package # default() adds the config entries a new Anki collection starts with collection = Collection.default() pkg = Package(collection=collection) See Package and collection for what they hold. 2. Create the notetypes A notetype takes a name, fields and templates. A template is a (name, front, back) tuple: API Models from genanki2 import deck, guid_for, note, notetype word = notetype( "Italian word", ["Italian", "English", "Audio"], [ ("Recognition", "{{Italian}}", "{{FrontSide}}
{{English}}"), ("Recall", "{{English}}", "{{FrontSide}}
{{Italian}}"), ("Listening", "{{Audio}}", "{{FrontSide}}
{{Italian}}"), ], id=1_759_600_000_000, css=".card { font-family: sans-serif; font-size: 28px; text-align: center; }", ) from genanki2 import Field, Notetype, NotetypeConfig, Template, TemplateConfig word = Notetype( id=1_759_600_000_000, name="Italian word", fields=[Field(name="Italian"), Field(name="English"), Field(name="Audio")], templates=[ Template( name="Recognition", config=TemplateConfig( q_format="{{Italian}}", a_format="{{FrontSide}}
{{English}}" ), ), Template( name="Recall", config=TemplateConfig( q_format="{{English}}", a_format="{{FrontSide}}
{{Italian}}" ), ), Template( name="Listening", config=TemplateConfig( q_format="{{Audio}}", a_format="{{FrontSide}}
{{Italian}}" ), ), ], config=NotetypeConfig( css=".card { font-family: sans-serif; font-size: 28px; text-align: center; }" ), ) Use cloze=True to make a cloze notetype (see Cloze notetypes ). Use sort_field="Italian" to set which field Anki's card browser "Sort Field" column shows. Any extra keyword arguments (such as css above) set options of the notetype's NotetypeConfig , which holds everything a notetype carries besides its name, fields and templates: its CSS, its sort field, the LaTeX preamble and postamble, and whether it is a cloze notetype. You cannot use kind , since cloze=True sets it. 3. Make the notes A note takes its notetype and one value per field, in the notetype's field order: API Models casa = note(word, ["casa", "house", ""], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")) mangiare = note( word, ["mangiare", "to eat", ""], tags=["verb"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "mangiare") ) from genanki2 import Note, guid_for casa = Note( notetype=word, fields=["casa", "house", ""], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa"), ) mangiare = Note( notetype=word, fields=["mangiare", "to eat", ""], tags=["verb"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "mangiare"), ) The notes above have no audio, so their "Listening" front is empty and they get two cards each, "Recognition" and "Recall". If you don't know the order of the fields and/or your fields are in a dictionary (for example, data read from a CSV file), you can use Notetype.field_values(mapping) to get them in the order the notetype expects: API Models # For fields missing from the map, the default value is an empty string values = word.field_values({"Italian": "finestra", "English": "window"}) finestra = note(word, values, tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "finestra")) # For fields missing from the map, the default value is an empty string values = word.field_values({"Italian": "finestra", "English": "window"}) finestra = Note( notetype=word, fields=values, tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "finestra") ) The notetype id and the note guids are explained in Identifiers that keep a deck updatable . 4. Create the decks deck() builds a normal deck: API Models vocabulary = deck("Italian::Vocabulary", description="Common words.") from genanki2 import DEFAULT_DECK_CONFIG, Deck, DeckNormalKind vocabulary = Deck( name="Italian::Vocabulary", kind=DeckNormalKind(description="Common words."), config=DEFAULT_DECK_CONFIG, # deck() gives a deck the default preset ) :: in a deck name makes a subdeck. Use the config parameter to set the deck preset. See Deck presets . Any extra keyword arguments set options of the deck's DeckNormalKind , which holds what a normal deck carries besides its name and preset: its description (and whether to render it as markdown), and the daily limits that override its preset's, such as new_limit and review_limit . 5. Add the notes to the collection collection.add_notes() makes the notes' cards in the deck you pass and then adds them in the collection: collection.add_notes([casa, mangiare], vocabulary) Add all the notes for a deck in one add_notes() call. Each call reads the whole collection, so a call per note becomes slow on a large deck. The notes are studied in the order they are added. Despite the name, add_notes() does not add notes in the collection.notes list. It only builds the cards and appends them in the collection.cards list. The method raises an error if notes that are already present in the collection have some cards (for those use collection.generate_missing_cards() ). The deck, the notetype and the notes do not have to be added manually to the lists: the cards refer to them, and the write process collects everything that the cards refer to using collection.collect_references() method. A manual call to any collection.collect_*() method will update the respective list/lists (although for a large collection, it can be expensive to repeatedly collect all references, that is why it is deferred until the write process needs it). Decks, notetypes and notes referenced by cards created with add_notes() and not already present in the collection will not be found by the collection's look up methods ( get_deck() , get_notetype() , etc.). For look ups to work, you need to either append them manually or collect the references after adding cards (the recommended way): collection.add_notes([casa, mangiare], vocabulary) collection.collect_decks() # or collection.collect_references() for everything assert collection.get_deck(name="Italian::Vocabulary") is not None 6. Add media Media files are added to the package by path and a field refers to them by file name: API Models pkg.media.append("audio/it_acqua.mp3") acqua = note( word, ["acqua", "water", "[sound:it_acqua.mp3]"], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "acqua"), ) collection.add_notes([acqua], vocabulary) # three cards, Listening included pkg.media.append("audio/it_acqua.mp3") acqua = Note( notetype=word, fields=["acqua", "water", "[sound:it_acqua.mp3]"], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "acqua"), ) collection.add_notes([acqua], vocabulary) # three cards, Listening included The write process raises an error if a note refers to a file missing from the pkg.media list and warns about unused files. pkg.trim_unused_media() drops those. To rename a file and every reference to it, see Renaming media . A build can also reuse the media files of another package without extracting them: pkg.add_source_media("italian.apkg") pkg.add_source_media(path) copies that package's files into this one when it is written. See Source packages for details. 7. Write the package pkg.write_apkg("italian.apkg") Before writing, genanki2 runs its checks and warnings over everything in the package. A check raises Genanki2Error for something Anki would reject or quietly change. A warning ( Genanki2Warning ) points at something Anki accepts but that is probably a mistake. Checks and warnings lists each one and shows how to run them before the write, and Settings shows how to turn them off. pkg.write_apkg(path) replaces a file that already exists at path. With overwrite=False it raises Genanki2Error instead. CollectionPackage.write_colpkg() and collection.write_sqlite() take the same argument. Field and template options A field that needs options can be built using the field() function and analogously a template with template() : API Models from genanki2 import field, template notes_field = field("Notes", collapsed=True, plain_text=True) translate_template = template( "Translate", "{{Italian}}", "{{FrontSide}}
{{English}}", a_format_browser="{{English}}", browser_font_size=18, ) phrase = notetype( "Italian phrase", ["Italian", "English", notes_field], [translate_template], id=1_759_600_000_001, sort_field="English", ) from genanki2 import ( Field, FieldConfig, Notetype, NotetypeConfig, Template, TemplateConfig, ) notes_field = Field(name="Notes", config=FieldConfig(collapsed=True, plain_text=True)) translate_template = Template( name="Translate", config=TemplateConfig( q_format="{{Italian}}", a_format="{{FrontSide}}
{{English}}", a_format_browser="{{English}}", browser_font_size=18, ), ) phrase = Notetype( id=1_759_600_000_001, name="Italian phrase", fields=[Field(name="Italian"), Field(name="English"), notes_field], templates=[translate_template], config=NotetypeConfig(sort_field_idx=1), # the position of "English" ) Any extra keyword arguments set options of the field's FieldConfig or of the template's TemplateConfig . A field's options are about Anki's note editor: its font, whether its value stays after a note is added ( sticky ), plain-text editing, and placeholder text ( description ). A template's options are about the card browser: the formats it shows instead of the card's sides ( q_format_browser , a_format_browser ) and its font. Cloze notetypes A cloze notetype makes one card per cloze number in the note, rather than one per template. Pass cloze=True , and use the cloze: filter on both sides of its one template: API Models cloze = notetype( "Italian cloze", ["Text", "Translation"], [("Cloze", "{{cloze:Text}}", "{{cloze:Text}}
{{Translation}}")], id=1_759_600_000_002, cloze=True, ) fields = [ "{{c1::Roma}} è la capitale d'{{c2::Italia}}.", "Rome is the capital of Italy.", ] collection.add_notes([note(cloze, fields)], vocabulary) # two cards cloze = Notetype( id=1_759_600_000_002, name="Italian cloze", fields=[Field(name="Text"), Field(name="Translation")], templates=[ Template( name="Cloze", config=TemplateConfig( q_format="{{cloze:Text}}", a_format="{{cloze:Text}}
{{Translation}}" ), ), ], # The cloze kind, with Anki's cloze styling config=NotetypeConfig.new_cloze_config(), ) fields = [ "{{c1::Roma}} è la capitale d'{{c2::Italia}}.", "Rome is the capital of Italy.", ] collection.add_notes([Note(notetype=cloze, fields=fields)], vocabulary) # two cards You can check the kind of a notetype using Notetype.is_cloze() / Notetype.is_normal() . Builtins genanki2 ships Anki's six stock notetypes: BASIC_NOTETYPE BASIC_AND_REVERSED_NOTETYPE BASIC_OPTIONAL_REVERSED_NOTETYPE BASIC_TYPE_IN_THE_ANSWER_NOTETYPE CLOZE_NOTETYPE IMAGE_OCCLUSION_NOTETYPE API Models from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE rome = note(BASIC_NOTETYPE, ["Capital of Italy?", "Rome"]) collection.add_notes([rome], vocabulary) from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE rome = Note(notetype=BASIC_NOTETYPE, fields=["Capital of Italy?", "Rome"]) collection.add_notes([rome], vocabulary) Every package that the program writes shares these constants, so they are read only: assigning to one raises an error. To change a builtin, change a copy instead: builtin_notetype("Basic (genanki2)", id=...) returns a new one on every call. Give the copy an id of its own that stays the same on every rebuild, since an import merges a notetype that keeps the stock id into the one the user already has. genanki2 also provides the default deck as DEFAULT_DECK and the default deck preset as DEFAULT_DECK_CONFIG . For example, you can add notes to the default deck: API Models from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE, DEFAULT_DECK paris = note(BASIC_NOTETYPE, ["Capital of France?", "Paris"]) collection.add_notes([paris], DEFAULT_DECK) from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE, DEFAULT_DECK paris = Note(notetype=BASIC_NOTETYPE, fields=["Capital of France?", "Paris"]) collection.add_notes([paris], DEFAULT_DECK) These constants are also immutable. You can build your own copies using default_deck() and default_deck_config() . Two more functions provide builtins: default_collection_metadata() : the default collection metadata that an empty collection contains. default_config_entries() : the default configurations of an empty collection. Deck presets A preset holds the study options, such as the number of new cards a day, and several decks can use the same one. Decks without one use Anki's default preset (which has id=1 ). Pass a preset to a deck as config : API Models from genanki2 import deck_config slow = deck_config("Italian, slow", id=1_759_600_000_100, new_per_day=5) grammar = deck("Italian::Grammar", config=slow) from genanki2 import DeckConfig, DeckConfigInner slow = DeckConfig( id=1_759_600_000_100, name="Italian, slow", config=DeckConfigInner(new_per_day=5) ) grammar = Deck(name="Italian::Grammar", config=slow) Anki only imports presets when the user ticks “Import any deck presets”. The import does not update the ones that the user already has. Anki matches presets by id, so give each one a fixed id. Any extra keyword arguments (such as new_per_day above) sets an option of the preset's DeckConfigInner , which holds how the preset schedules the decks that use it: the daily limits ( new_per_day , reviews_per_day ), the learning steps in minutes ( learn_steps , relearn_steps ), maximum_review_interval , desired_retention and the burying options. An option that is not given keeps the value that Anki gives a new preset. Filtered decks A filtered deck gathers cards from normal decks by a search, written in the syntax of Anki's browser. filtered_deck() builds one: API Models from genanki2 import filtered_deck cram = filtered_deck("Italian::Cram verbs", search="deck:Italian tag:verb", limit=50) from genanki2 import DeckFilteredKind SearchTerm = DeckFilteredKind.SearchTerm cram = Deck( name="Italian::Cram verbs", kind=DeckFilteredKind( search_terms=[ SearchTerm( search="deck:Italian tag:verb", limit=50, order=SearchTerm.Order.RANDOM ), ], ), ) Up to limit cards are gathered using search , ordered by order (random by default). search2 adds a second search, with its own limit2 and order2 . With reschedule=False , the deck is a preview: answering a card there does not change its schedule. A filtered deck has no preset, and collection.add_notes() refuses one, because a card belongs to a normal deck first. Anki fills a filtered deck when the user builds it and an .apkg import drops empty decks. So a filtered deck written to an .apkg reaches the user only when it holds a card and it stays filtered only when the user ticks "Import any learning progress". Otherwise the import turns it into a normal deck. A card goes into a filtered deck with the filtered deck as Card.deck and its home deck as Card.original_deck , assigned in that order, since a card in a normal deck has its home deck cleared: API Models bere = note( word, ["bere", "to drink", ""], tags=["verb"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "bere") ) recognition, recall = collection.add_notes([bere], vocabulary)[0] recognition.deck, recognition.original_deck = cram, recognition.deck bere = Note( notetype=word, fields=["bere", "to drink", ""], tags=["verb"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "bere"), ) recognition, recall = collection.add_notes([bere], vocabulary)[0] recognition.deck, recognition.original_deck = cram, recognition.deck A collection package carries filtered decks as they are. See Collection packages . Customizing cards collection.add_notes() returns the new cards, grouped per note, in the order of the notes. Use them to change a card before it is written: API Models from genanki2 import CardFlag notes = [note(word, ["cane", "dog", ""], guid=guid_for(word.id, "cane"))] for recognition, recall in collection.add_notes(notes, vocabulary): recognition.flags = CardFlag.RED recall.suspend() from genanki2 import CardFlag notes = [ Note(notetype=word, fields=["cane", "dog", ""], guid=guid_for(word.id, "cane")) ] for recognition, recall in collection.add_notes(notes, vocabulary): recognition.flags = CardFlag.RED recall.suspend() card.flags holds the colour flag that Anki's browser shows, one of the CardFlag values from RED to PURPLE , or NONE . suspend() keeps a card out of the reviews until the user unsuspends it. bury() keeps it out for the rest of the day instead: Anki unburies it at the next day rollover. A card's state reaches the user only when they tick "Import any learning progress" while importing. Without it, which is the default, Anki imports every card as a new card, unsuspended and without flags, keeping only its position. A note gets the cards that Anki would give it: one for each template whose front is not empty. A note whose fronts are all empty still gets the first template's card, with a warning. The full rules are in Card generation .

docs.text: genanki2 ships Anki's six stock notetypes: BASIC_NOTETYPE BASIC_AND_REVERSED_NOTETYPE BASIC_OPTIONAL_REVERSED_NOTETYPE BASIC_TYPE_IN_THE_ANSWER_NOTETYPE CLOZE_NOTETYPE IMAGE_OCCLUSION_NOTETYPE API Models from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE rome = note(BASIC_NOTETYPE, ["Capital of Italy?", "Rome"]) collection.add_notes([rome], vocabulary) from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE rome = Note(notetype=BASIC_NOTETYPE, fields=["Capital of Italy?", "Rome"]) collection.add_notes([rome], vocabulary) Every package that the program writes shares these constants, so they are read only: assigning to one raises an error. To change a builtin, change a copy instead: builtin_notetype("Basic (genanki2)", id=...) returns a new one on every call. Give the copy an id of its own that stays the same on every rebuild, since an import merges a notetype that keeps the stock id into the one the user already has. genanki2 also provides the default deck as DEFAULT_DECK and the default deck preset as DEFAULT_DECK_CONFIG . For example, you can add notes to the default deck: API Models from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE, DEFAULT_DECK paris = note(BASIC_NOTETYPE, ["Capital of France?", "Paris"]) collection.add_notes([paris], DEFAULT_DECK) from genanki2 import BASIC_NOTETYPE, DEFAULT_DECK paris = Note(notetype=BASIC_NOTETYPE, fields=["Capital of France?", "Paris"]) collection.add_notes([paris], DEFAULT_DECK) These constants are also immutable. You can build your own copies using default_deck() and default_deck_config() . Two more functions provide builtins: default_collection_metadata() : the default collection metadata that an empty collection contains. default_config_entries() : the default configurations of an empty collection.
docs.title: Builtins

docs.text: A preset holds the study options, such as the number of new cards a day, and several decks can use the same one. Decks without one use Anki's default preset (which has id=1 ). Pass a preset to a deck as config : API Models from genanki2 import deck_config slow = deck_config("Italian, slow", id=1_759_600_000_100, new_per_day=5) grammar = deck("Italian::Grammar", config=slow) from genanki2 import DeckConfig, DeckConfigInner slow = DeckConfig( id=1_759_600_000_100, name="Italian, slow", config=DeckConfigInner(new_per_day=5) ) grammar = Deck(name="Italian::Grammar", config=slow) Anki only imports presets when the user ticks “Import any deck presets”. The import does not update the ones that the user already has. Anki matches presets by id, so give each one a fixed id. Any extra keyword arguments (such as new_per_day above) sets an option of the preset's DeckConfigInner , which holds how the preset schedules the decks that use it: the daily limits ( new_per_day , reviews_per_day ), the learning steps in minutes ( learn_steps , relearn_steps ), maximum_review_interval , desired_retention and the burying options. An option that is not given keeps the value that Anki gives a new preset.
docs.title: Deck presets

docs.text: A filtered deck gathers cards from normal decks by a search, written in the syntax of Anki's browser. filtered_deck() builds one: API Models from genanki2 import filtered_deck cram = filtered_deck("Italian::Cram verbs", search="deck:Italian tag:verb", limit=50) from genanki2 import DeckFilteredKind SearchTerm = DeckFilteredKind.SearchTerm cram = Deck( name="Italian::Cram verbs", kind=DeckFilteredKind( search_terms=[ SearchTerm( search="deck:Italian tag:verb", limit=50, order=SearchTerm.Order.RANDOM ), ], ), ) Up to limit cards are gathered using search , ordered by order (random by default). search2 adds a second search, with its own limit2 and order2 . With reschedule=False , the deck is a preview: answering a card there does not change its schedule. A filtered deck has no preset, and collection.add_notes() refuses one, because a card belongs to a normal deck first. Anki fills a filtered deck when the user builds it and an .apkg import drops empty decks. So a filtered deck written to an .apkg reaches the user only when it holds a card and it stays filtered only when the user ticks "Import any learning progress". Otherwise the import turns it into a normal deck. A card goes into a filtered deck with the filtered deck as Card.deck and its home deck as Card.original_deck , assigned in that order, since a card in a normal deck has its home deck cleared: API Models bere = note( word, ["bere", "to drink", ""], tags=["verb"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "bere") ) recognition, recall = collection.add_notes([bere], vocabulary)[0] recognition.deck, recognition.original_deck = cram, recognition.deck bere = Note( notetype=word, fields=["bere", "to drink", ""], tags=["verb"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "bere"), ) recognition, recall = collection.add_notes([bere], vocabulary)[0] recognition.deck, recognition.original_deck = cram, recognition.deck A collection package carries filtered decks as they are. See Collection packages .
docs.title: Filtered decks

docs.text: collection.add_notes() returns the new cards, grouped per note, in the order of the notes. Use them to change a card before it is written: API Models from genanki2 import CardFlag notes = [note(word, ["cane", "dog", ""], guid=guid_for(word.id, "cane"))] for recognition, recall in collection.add_notes(notes, vocabulary): recognition.flags = CardFlag.RED recall.suspend() from genanki2 import CardFlag notes = [ Note(notetype=word, fields=["cane", "dog", ""], guid=guid_for(word.id, "cane")) ] for recognition, recall in collection.add_notes(notes, vocabulary): recognition.flags = CardFlag.RED recall.suspend() card.flags holds the colour flag that Anki's browser shows, one of the CardFlag values from RED to PURPLE , or NONE . suspend() keeps a card out of the reviews until the user unsuspends it. bury() keeps it out for the rest of the day instead: Anki unburies it at the next day rollover. A card's state reaches the user only when they tick "Import any learning progress" while importing. Without it, which is the default, Anki imports every card as a new card, unsuspended and without flags, keeping only its position. A note gets the cards that Anki would give it: one for each template whose front is not empty. A note whose fronts are all empty still gets the first template's card, with a warning. The full rules are in Card generation .
docs.title: Customizing cards

docs.text: Checks and warnings genanki2 validates a package (and any model) before writing it, so a problem is raised in your script, not when importing in Anki or when reviewing cards. It does so in two ways: A check raises Genanki2Error for something that Anki would reject or quietly change, or that would break later, when reviewing cards. A warning ( Genanki2Warning ) points at something that Anki accepts but which is probably a mistake. This page explains when they run and how to call them by hand, then lists every check and warning by model. How they work When a serialization method is called on a model, three phases run before the actual serialization: Prepare makes the model ready to be written: Timestamping edited notes and notetypes; updating the collection's list with all the referenced decks, notes, notetypes, etc.; running some of Anki's database check repairs; Check runs the checks. Some checks raise if the preparation phase is skipped. Warn runs the warnings. The serialization methods include: Package.write_apkg() , CollectionPackage.write_colpkg() , Collection.write_sqlite() and a model's to_row() , to_rows() or to_bytes() . Each phase is recursive by default, reaching every model inside the serialized model and running on each of them once. Use recursive=False to limit them to the model's own steps. Example: a card reaches its note and its deck, card.check() calls all of its checks, then calls note.check() and deck.check() if recursive is True . checks_disabled() and warnings_disabled() skip the checks and the warnings of a write (see Settings ). The preparation always runs, except on a frozen model because freeze() already prepared it. The phases can also be run by hand: from genanki2 import Package, guid_for pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) word = pkg.collection.get_notetype(name="Italian word") casa = pkg.collection.get_note(guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")) pkg.prepare().check() # the package and every model it holds word.check(recursive=False) # the notetype's own checks, not its fields' or templates' word.check_unique_fronts() # a single check casa.warn() # the note's warnings, and its notetype's Each check and warning in the tables below is also a public method that runs alone. A manual call to a phase or a specific method runs regardless of the settings. A few details: Call collection.prepare() or collection.collect_references() before calling check() by hand on a collection (or the package holding it). The collection's lists hold only what was read or added to them. If some referenced objects are missing from the lists, collection.check_referential_integrity() will raise. pkg.write_apkg() and colpkg.write_colpkg() tell the phases which kind of file they write (using a SerializationContext parameter) because some checks and warnings apply only to one of them, as the tables indicate. During a manual call without context, the checks that apply only to a .colpkg are skipped, and the warnings that depend on the kind of file written describe both outcomes. Some values are repaired rather than refused (see Repairs ). Several warnings below report a value that a repair would have changed and are emitted only when the repairs are off (inside dbcheck_repairs_disabled() ). Package and media Package Check/Warning Description check_media_paths Each media file exists, is readable, and has a name that Anki can store as it is and that no other file in media has. Also runs when media is assigned. check_builtin_notetype_versions A builtin notetype keeps the version Anki gave it as its modification time. A larger value would overwrite the user's copy of that builtin on import. check_media_references_are_present Every file that a note, a notetype's CSS or a template refers to is in the package. Lists the missing ones, and the renames that fix references to a source package's repaired names. warn_unused_media_files A file in the package that nothing refers to. It imports, but takes space. Names beginning with _ are exempt. Only a warning, since a restore keeps the files already in the user's media folder. MediaEntries The media map that a package writes, built by genanki2 itself. Anki would rename one of them. both check_unique_tags No two tags differ only in case. both check_unique_card_producers No two cards come from the same note and template. Otherwise the restored collection cannot be studied until Anki updates it, or cannot be opened at all. .colpkg warn_future_ids A note, card or review id more than a day in the future. A future one blocks updates until it passes. warn_empty_card_generation A front that can never make a card, for any note. warn_unused_fields A field that no template shows. Template Check/Warning Description check_templates_parse Each side parses: every conditional that is opened is closed, under the same name. check_min_front_references The front refers to at least one field. Anki refuses a front that shows the same text for every note. warn_misleading_target_deck_id A deck override that an import breaks, since it gives decks new ids. Only for an .apkg . Anki cannot detect duplicates of such a note. warn_normal_note_cloze_field Cloze markup in a note whose notetype is not a cloze one. It shows as written. warn_cloze_on_wrong_field Cloze markup in a field that the cloze template does not pass through cloze: . It makes a card with nothing hidden. warn_mod_time_in_future A modification time in the future, which blocks updates until it passes. Only with the repairs off. warn_unimported_changes A change to a read note that an import skips, because its modification time is not newer than the read one. Deck The deck's kind, DeckNormalKind or DeckFilteredKind , is checked along with it. Check/Warning Description check_normal_kind_config_id A normal deck's kind.config_id is its preset's id. sync_normal_kind_config_id() copies it. check_mod_time_not_in_future The modification time has already happened. A future one blocks updates until it passes. warn_unimported_changes A change to a read deck that an import never applies, such as emptying its description or clearing a limit. DeckNormalKind.warn_bad_desired_retention A desired retention outside 0.7 to 0.99, which Anki uses as given. DeckFilteredKind.warn_too_many_search_terms More than two searches. Anki reads only the first two. SearchTerm.warn_int_value_in_enum_field A search order that its enum does not name. Anki falls back to the first order. DeckConfig The preset's options, DeckConfigInner , are checked along with it. Check/Warning Description check_mod_time_not_in_future The modification time has already happened. A future one blocks updates until it passes. warn_unsearchable_name A name that the FSRS optimizer cannot search for, when the preset sets no search of its own. warn_unimported_changes A change to a read preset that an import never applies, since Anki does not update a preset the user already has. DeckConfigInner.check_learning_steps Each learning step is between 0 and 2**31 // 60 minutes. DeckConfigInner.check_fsrs_params_length The FSRS parameters have a length FSRS can take. Otherwise no deck using the preset can be studied. DeckConfigInner.check_date ignore_revlogs_before_date is empty or a date. DeckConfigInner.check_easy_days_percentages easy_days_percentages is empty or has 7 values. Otherwise no deck can be studied. DeckConfigInner.warn_int_value_in_enum_field An option holding a number its enum does not name. Anki falls back to the option's first value. Card The card's data (a CardData ) is checked along with it. Check/Warning Description check_template_ordinal The card's template ordinal is one of its notetype's templates. Not checked on a cloze notetype, where it names a cloze number. check_due_not_a_timestamp A due that counts days does not hold a timestamp. An import would shift it centuries away. check_original_due_not_a_timestamp The same, for original_due . check_original_deck_is_normal The card's original deck is not a filtered deck. check_mod_time_not_in_future The modification time has already happened. A future one blocks updates until it passes. warn_due_above_ceiling A new card position of 2,000,000 or more. Only with the repairs off. warn_graduated_card_without_ease_factor A review or relearning card with no ease factor. With SM-2, its interval barely grows. warn_unexplained_original_due An original due with no original deck. Only with the repairs off. warn_unexplained_original_data An original deck and due on a card that is not in a filtered deck. Only with the repairs off. warn_template_ord_above_ceiling A template ordinal above 30,000. Only with the repairs off. warn_interval_days_above_ceiling An interval above 2**31 - 1 days. Only with the repairs off. warn_unimported_changes A change to a read card that an import never applies, since Anki never updates a card the user has. CardData.check_custom_data Custom data that Anki can store. Anki checks it only when the card is answered. CardData.warn_unpaired_stability_difficulty An FSRS stability without a difficulty, or the other way round. The scheduler ignores it. History and settings Review Check/Warning Description warn_rescheduled_typed_as_learning A learning review with no answer and no time. Anki's database check retypes it as a reschedule. warn_review_type_and_ease_disagree A review type and a button that Anki never writes together. FSRS reads the button. warn_time_above_ceiling An answer time above 2**31 - 1. Only with the repairs off. warn_int_value_in_enum_field A type or button that its enum does not name. Grave Check/Warning Description check_default_deck_is_not_deleted No grave deletes deck 1. A sync would delete the default deck everywhere. CollectionMetadata Check/Warning Description check_creation_time_not_in_future The collection's creation time has already happened. Review cards count their due day from it. ConfigEntry Check/Warning Description warn_unloadable_value A config value that is not JSON. Anki uses the built-in default instead. Checks outside the phases A few checks run at another time, and raise at once: When a value is assigned: a deck with id 1 cannot be filtered, a filtered deck cannot have a preset, and media is checked by check_media_paths . Every attribute is also validated for its type and range. When a package is read: each row has to agree with the objects it is read with (a card with its note and deck, a note with its notetype, a review with its card), a notetype's fields and templates have to be numbered 0 to n-1, the collection has to be schema v18, and the media map has to name files the package carries. The read also warns about two media files with the same name, and about files stored under a repaired name.

docs.text: Concepts An Anki package ( .apkg ) is a zip file that holds a small Anki collection and the media files that notes refer to. This page describes the objects genanki2 uses to model it and the identifiers that make a new version of a deck import as an update and not make duplicates. Package and collection A package holds a small Anki collection and genanki2 models it with the same objects that Anki uses. package() returns two objects: The package holds the media files and handles reading and writing to disk, through Package.read_apkg() and pkg.write_apkg() . The collection holds the decks, notetypes, notes and cards, among other things. It can also be read and written to disk, independently of the package, using Collection.read_sqlite() and collection.write_sqlite() . API Models from genanki2 import package pkg, collection = package() from genanki2 import Collection, Package collection = Collection() # An empty collection # Although Anki does not start from a completely empty collection. # default() adds the default config entries, which are required collection = Collection.default() # anki_default() also adds the default deck, preset and builtin notetypes, but are technically optional collection = Collection.anki_default() pkg = Package(collection=collection) Package A package has two attributes: pkg.collection : the collection it writes. pkg.media : the paths of the media files it writes. A field refers to a file by its file name only, so two paths ending in the same name collide: pkg.media.append("audio/it_casa.mp3") pkg.media.append("more_audio/it_casa.mp3") # Raises on the media check A package (called "source") read with keep_source_media=True keeps track of media files in it and adds them to the written package, but in a separate list. See Reading a package . Use Package.read_apkg() and pkg.write_apkg() for disk I/O. A CollectionPackage is basically the same thing (same attributes, mostly the same methods), but it is interpreted as a whole collection backup and uses a different file extension, .colpkg . See Collection packages . Collection The collection holds a list per table, either what was read or added manually: collection.deck_configs for deck presets collection.decks for decks collection.notetypes for notetypes. A notetype contains all of its fields and templates inside it, so there are no dedicated lists for them. collection.notes for notes collection.tags for tags (this is ignored during import; it is present only for completeness' sake) collection.cards for cards collection.reviews for revision history collection.graves for deleted objects (also ignored) collection.config for configuration entries collection.metadata for metadata, like creation time (this is always a 1 row table) The lists do not have to be filled by hand. add_notes() adds the cards to collection.cards , and the write process collects everything the cards refer to: the notes, their notetypes, the decks and the decks' presets. See Building a deck . Some relevant methods: add_notes() returns the new cards, so they can be changed before a write (see Customizing cards ). generate_missing_cards() makes the cards that an edit adds, and remove_notes() removes notes together with their cards (see Cards after an edit and Removing notes ). To find objects, use the lookup methods such as collection.get_deck(name=...) and collection.get_note(guid=...) (see Reading a package ). Collection.read_sqlite() and collection.write_sqlite() for disk I/O. You can read only the collection inside a package using Collection.from_apkg() . A collection's objects Notetypes, fields and templates A notetype says which fields a note has and which cards it produces. Each card type is a template , with a front and a back written in Anki's template syntax. A notetype is either standard or cloze. A cloze notetype has a single template and makes one card per cloze number in the note ( {{c1::...}} , {{c2::...}} ). See Cloze notetypes . API Models from genanki2 import notetype # A template is a (name, front, back) tuple word = notetype( "Italian word", ["Italian", "English"], [("Recognition", "{{Italian}}", "{{FrontSide}}<hr id=answer>{{English}}")], id=1_759_600_000_000, ) from genanki2 import Field, Notetype, Template, TemplateConfig word = Notetype( id=1_759_600_000_000, name="Italian word", fields=[Field(name="Italian"), Field(name="English")], templates=[ Template( name="Recognition", config=TemplateConfig( q_format="{{Italian}}", # the front a_format="{{FrontSide}}<hr id=answer>{{English}}", # the back ), ), ], ) Notes A note is one entry: a value for each field of its notetype. note.fields holds the values in the order of the notetype's fields, and note["English"] reads or sets one by name. The values are HTML, and a note refers to a media file by its name, as in [sound:it_casa.mp3] (see Building a deck ). API Models from genanki2 import guid_for, note casa = note(word, ["casa", "house"], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")) from genanki2 import Note, guid_for casa = Note( notetype=word, fields=["casa", "house"], tags=["noun"], guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa"), ) Decks and presets A deck holds cards. Its study options come from a preset (in Anki's interface, the deck's Options). :: in a name makes a subdeck: Italian::Vocabulary is Vocabulary inside Italian . A deck is either normal or filtered: A normal deck owns its cards and has a preset. A filtered deck has no preset: it gathers cards from normal decks by a search, so they can be studied apart for a while, and they return to their home deck when it is emptied. A card in a filtered deck has the filtered deck as card.deck and its home deck as card.original_deck . Use deck.is_normal() / deck.is_filtered() to tell them apart. Filtered decks are usually built by users in Anki, so they mostly show up when reading someone's collection backup. See Filtered decks on building one. API Models from genanki2 import deck, deck_config slow = deck_config("Italian, slow", id=1_759_600_000_100, new_per_day=5) vocabulary = deck("Italian::Vocabulary", config=slow) from genanki2 import Deck, DeckConfig, DeckConfigInner slow = DeckConfig( id=1_759_600_000_100, name="Italian, slow", config=DeckConfigInner(new_per_day=5) ) vocabulary = Deck(name="Italian::Vocabulary", config=slow) Cards A card is one thing to study. A note gets one card per template whose front is not empty, or one card per cloze number on a cloze notetype. A card holds the study progress ( card_type , queue , due , interval_days and others), so this is where a user's schedule lives. Every card in a newly built package is new. API Models # One tuple of cards per note, with a card for each template that renders cards = collection.add_notes([casa], vocabulary) recognition = cards[0][0] from genanki2 import Card # The template's position, and the new-card position add_notes() would give recognition = Card(note=casa, deck=vocabulary, template_ord=0, due=1) collection.cards.append(recognition) Identifiers that keep a deck updatable When someone imports a new version of a deck that they already have, Anki decides what is an update by comparing identifiers: notetypes by id and then their fields and templates, by id (if present) or by name notes by guid decks by name presets by id An object whose identifier changed between versions arrives as a second copy, next to the first. You can spot them because Anki appends a "+" to the name (something similar to "My Notetype" and "My Notetype+"). A deck that will be rebuilt needs identifiers that stay the same on every build: Notetype ids. Without id= , notetype() makes a new one each run using the monotonic_id() function. Pass a fixed number, any integer chosen once. A millisecond timestamp is what Anki uses. Field and template ids. A notetype whose fields or templates change (added, removed, reordered, or renamed without an id) arrives as a copy even with the same notetype id. Notetype.fill_missing_ids() gives them ids, but random ones, so a rebuild script should call it only in the first build or should pass fixed ones ( field("Italian", id=...) ). See Changing a notetype's fields or templates . Note guids. Without guid= , a note gets a random one each run using the guid() function. guid_for(notetype.id, key) derives a guid from a stable key that names the note in your data: a word, a row id, a file name. Pass several key parts when no single one is unique ( guid_for(notetype.id, key1, key2, ...) ). Do not derive it from the whole note: a corrected translation would then change the guid, and the corrected note would arrive as a duplicate beside the old one. Deck names have to stay the same. A renamed deck arrives as a new deck, and the cards that users already have stay in the old one. Alternatively, build a deck only once , the first time, and never rebuild it again. Any updates you need to make can be done by a read-update-write flow using genanki2 (see Updating a package ). Thus, you don't have to hardcode and keep track of unique ids or guids. Cards have no identifier of their own: the import never updates a card that a user already has, as Changing cards explains.

docs.text: Reading a package genanki2 reads packages that use the latest database schema (v18) and any package format. It does not read Anki's "Support older Anki versions" export, which uses the old collection format (v11). Reading a package validates every table and repairs a few values the way Anki does when it saves them; Repairs lists them. from genanki2 import Package pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) collection = pkg.collection The collection contains lists for everything it holds (decks, presets, notetypes, notes, etc.), either read or added manually. See Package and collection for the full details. It also has a few lists for orphaned objects (fields, templates, notes, cards and reviews). These are objects referencing other objects which are not present in the database and cannot be modeled. The collection has lookup methods to find single objects: collection.get_config_entry(key) collection.get_deck_config() , by id or by name collection.get_deck() , by id or by name collection.get_notetype() , by id or by name collection.get_note() , by id or by guid In case a lookup method cannot find what you are looking for, try a manual search in the corresponding orphan list ( collection.orphan_* ). Example: vocabulary = collection.get_deck(name="Italian::Vocabulary") word = collection.get_notetype(name="Italian word") casa = collection.get_note(guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")) for note in collection.notes: print(note["Italian"], note.tags) examples/read_package.py prints a summary of a package. Managing media files Media files can be read in 2 ways: Using extract_dir="..." writes all the media files to a folder. This allows inspecting the media files and replacing them easily on the disk. As a consequence, pkg.media holds their paths after the reading finished. An extracted file replaces a file of the same name already in the directory. With overwrite=False , the read raises Genanki2Error instead and extracts nothing. extract_dir has a secondary effect: it also extracts the collection database in the same directory. It is an SQLite file named collection.anki21b (according to the latest package format; .anki2 or .anki21 for the older package formats). This makes it convenient to explore the database using specialized software or alter it using scripts (for example, using genanki2's Collection.read_sqlite() and collection.write_sqlite() ). The SQLite file is ignored by the write process. Using keep_source_media=True leaves them in the source file, but keeps track of them. The next write process copies them from the source file into the newly written package. This makes it easy to correct some notes or add some new ones, without having to extract them and occupy disk space. Of course, this behaviour only works if the source file is still present during the write and hasn't changed since the read. The package is written to another path: writing over the source file is refused (details here ). With neither, the package is read without its media. A warning is shown that media files have been ignored and that writing the package back refuses any note that refers to a file (in this case, pkg.media is an empty list). Source packages A source package is a package whose media files are copied when this package is written. Reading with keep_source_media=True makes the package being read the source. pkg.add_source_media(path) sets one on any package, read or newly built, for example to reuse the media files of the last release in a fresh build without extracting them: API Models from genanki2 import package pkg, collection = package() pkg.add_source_media("italian.apkg") from genanki2 import Collection, Package pkg = Package(collection=Collection.default()) pkg.add_source_media("italian.apkg") Notes can refer to the source's files as to any file in pkg.media , and the write counts them as carried. The files stay in the source until the write, so it has to still be present and unchanged then. A file in pkg.media with the same name as a file in the source is written instead of it ( pkg.media has priority over the source's media). An unused source file is warned about and pkg.trim_unused_media() drops it as it drops the unused files in pkg.media . Names that Anki would not store are repaired as on a read, with the same warning. A package has a single source, so adding one replaces the previous one. add_source_media() raises if the package at path carries no media files. If you want to combine media from multiple packages, either extract all the media files, then write one containing all, or perform multiple steps of read->add_source_media()->write, each step reading the package from the last step and adding media from another package. pkg.remove_source_media() removes the source, so the next write copies nothing from it. Collection packages An .apkg is a shared deck (or decks) and merges into the collection of whoever imports it. A .colpkg is an export of a user's entire collection. When imported, it replaces their whole collection. This is what Anki writes for "Export collection" and for its backups. genanki2 models this with CollectionPackage . Its methods CollectionPackage.read_colpkg() and colpkg.write_colpkg() read and write one, for changing your own collection or backup. A restore doesn't repair anything. Anki replaces the collection and marks the schema as modified, so the next sync is a one-way full upload. Media files are added, never removed. Anki saves to disk each file that the .colpkg carries unless the media folder already holds an equal one. A backup can hold thousands of files: read_colpkg(path, keep_source_media=True) followed by write_colpkg() to a new path copies them without extracting them. The file name decides the import. Anki restores any file ending in .colpkg or named collection.apkg or backup-*.apkg , and merges every other .apkg . write_apkg() refuses those three names, since a deck written under one of them would replace the collection of whoever imports it, and write_colpkg() refuses a name without the .colpkg suffix. write_colpkg() writes the latest package format only. Anki's "Support older Anki versions" collection export uses schema 11, which genanki2 does not read. The API does not provide a method to create a collection package. One built from scratch needs all the defaults that Anki adds to an empty collection. Use this recipe: from genanki2 import Collection, CollectionPackage colpkg = CollectionPackage(collection=Collection.anki_default()) Read errors A failed read raises one of two errors, both subclasses of Genanki2Error : PackageReadError : the file is not a package genanki2 can make sense of. It is not a zip file, it carries neither a meta entry nor a collection entry, an entry does not decompress, or its media map does not parse. A write raises it too when the source package of its media is gone or has changed since it was added. It uses another schema version (such as the v11 that "Support older Anki versions" exports), misses a table or a column, or holds rows that do not fit together, such as a notetype whose fields are not numbered from 0. If genanki2 still cannot read the export, try to fix the values in Anki. If Anki also refuses the import, extract the package and edit the database by hand. docs.text: genanki2 reads packages that use the latest database schema (v18) and any package format. It does not read Anki's "Support older Anki versions" export, which uses the old collection format (v11). Reading a package validates every table and repairs a few values the way Anki does when it saves them; Repairs lists them. from genanki2 import Package pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) collection = pkg.collection The collection contains lists for everything it holds (decks, presets, notetypes, notes, etc.), either read or added manually. See Package and collection for the full details. It also has a few lists for orphaned objects (fields, templates, notes, cards and reviews). These are objects referencing other objects which are not present in the database and cannot be modeled. The collection has lookup methods to find single objects: collection.get_config_entry(key) collection.get_deck_config() , by id or by name collection.get_deck() , by id or by name collection.get_notetype() , by id or by name collection.get_note() , by id or by guid In case a lookup method cannot find what you are looking for, try a manual search in the corresponding orphan list ( collection.orphan_* ). Example: vocabulary = collection.get_deck(name="Italian::Vocabulary") word = collection.get_notetype(name="Italian word") casa = collection.get_note(guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")) for note in collection.notes: print(note["Italian"], note.tags) examples/read_package.py prints a summary of a package.

docs.text: Media files can be read in 2 ways: Using extract_dir="..." writes all the media files to a folder. This allows inspecting the media files and replacing them easily on the disk. As a consequence, pkg.media holds their paths after the reading finished. An extracted file replaces a file of the same name already in the directory. With overwrite=False , the read raises Genanki2Error instead and extracts nothing. extract_dir has a secondary effect: it also extracts the collection database in the same directory. It is an SQLite file named collection.anki21b (according to the latest package format; .anki2 or .anki21 for the older package formats). This makes it convenient to explore the database using specialized software or alter it using scripts (for example, using genanki2's Collection.read_sqlite() and collection.write_sqlite() ). The SQLite file is ignored by the write process. Using keep_source_media=True leaves them in the source file, but keeps track of them. The next write process copies them from the source file into the newly written package. This makes it easy to correct some notes or add some new ones, without having to extract them and occupy disk space. Of course, this behaviour only works if the source file is still present during the write and hasn't changed since the read. The package is written to another path: writing over the source file is refused (details here ). With neither, the package is read without its media. A warning is shown that media files have been ignored and that writing the package back refuses any note that refers to a file (in this case, pkg.media is an empty list).

docs.text: A source package is a package whose media files are copied when this package is written. Reading with keep_source_media=True makes the package being read the source. pkg.add_source_media(path) sets one on any package, read or newly built, for example to reuse the media files of the last release in a fresh build without extracting them: API Models from genanki2 import package pkg, collection = package() pkg.add_source_media("italian.apkg") from genanki2 import Collection, Package pkg = Package(collection=Collection.default()) pkg.add_source_media("italian.apkg") Notes can refer to the source's files as to any file in pkg.media , and the write counts them as carried. The files stay in the source until the write, so it has to still be present and unchanged then. A file in pkg.media with the same name as a file in the source is written instead of it ( pkg.media has priority over the source's media). An unused source file is warned about and pkg.trim_unused_media() drops it as it drops the unused files in pkg.media . Names that Anki would not store are repaired as on a read, with the same warning. A package has a single source, so adding one replaces the previous one. add_source_media() raises if the package at path carries no media files. If you want to combine media from multiple packages, either extract all the media files, then write one containing all, or perform multiple steps of read->add_source_media()->write, each step reading the package from the last step and adding media from another package. pkg.remove_source_media() removes the source, so the next write copies nothing from it.

docs.text: An .apkg is a shared deck (or decks) and merges into the collection of whoever imports it. A .colpkg is an export of a user's entire collection. When imported, it replaces their whole collection. This is what Anki writes for "Export collection" and for its backups. genanki2 models this with CollectionPackage . Its methods CollectionPackage.read_colpkg() and colpkg.write_colpkg() read and write one, for changing your own collection or backup. A restore doesn't repair anything. Anki replaces the collection and marks the schema as modified, so the next sync is a one-way full upload. Media files are added, never removed. Anki saves to disk each file that the .colpkg carries unless the media folder already holds an equal one. A backup can hold thousands of files: read_colpkg(path, keep_source_media=True) followed by write_colpkg() to a new path copies them without extracting them. The file name decides the import. Anki restores any file ending in .colpkg or named collection.apkg or backup-*.apkg , and merges every other .apkg . write_apkg() refuses those three names, since a deck written under one of them would replace the collection of whoever imports it, and write_colpkg() refuses a name without the .colpkg suffix. write_colpkg() writes the latest package format only. One built from scratch needs all the defaults that Anki adds to an empty collection. Use this recipe: from genanki2 import Collection, CollectionPackage colpkg = CollectionPackage(collection=Collection.anki_default())

docs.text: Repairs genanki2 changes automatically some of the values it is given or it reads. Most of these changes would happen anyway: Anki silently updates the value on an import, on a save or when "Check Database" is run. Any genanki2 repair that mirrors what "Check Database" does emits a warning. Other repairs available in genanki2 are opt in. Many warnings and errors name the call, or the edit, that makes them go away. This page lists the automatic and opt in repairs and how to solve errors and warnings. The reasons behind each automatic repair, and where Anki makes the same one, are in Repairs that alter what they read . Automatic repairs Normalized values on save These run whenever a value is set, whether by the caller or by a read, and they never warn . Anki would make each change itself, so the package imports the same either way. Normalizing names and text: deck names, tags, notetype names, field names and template names; notes.sfld and csum : a note's sort field and checksum are recomputed from its fields on every write; Out-of-range preset values: 18 preset scalars go back to their default when set outside the range that Anki accepts. The learning and relearning steps are clamped to the nearest bound. Unreadable dues and durations: Card.due and Card.original_due outside the 32-bit signed range, and Review.time_ms outside the 32-bit unsigned range, become 0 , which is what Anki reads in their place. A normal deck's preset id: a deck's Deck.config.id (if set) has priority over Deck.kind.config_id , which gets overwritten; Normalizing media file names: extraction and keep_source_media=True store each file under the normalized name (using normalize_media_name() ), with a suffix when two names repair to the same one. The references in notes, CSS and templates are not updated and a warning lists the renames to apply (see Media references below). A validator runs when a field is assigned, but there are some edge cases. One such case is mutable containers which don't trigger them, so a list changed in place is not repaired. Examples: DeckConfig.config.learn_steps.append(...) skips the clamp and the write refuses the steps with a message asking to assign the list back. Changing Deck.kind.config_id directly skips the preset id copy and the write refuses the deck until Deck.sync_normal_kind_config_id() runs. Anki's "Check Database" Anki stores these values until the user runs Tools > Check Database. genanki2 repairs them when set or read and warns each time about it. A repair called inside the block works, so specific fixes can be applied. dbcheck_repairs_enabled() turns the repairs back on inside a disabled block. A card's original deck and due are checked again once the decks are final, as in the table above. Opt in repairs Nothing in this section is called inside genanki2. Media references Reading a package can rename media files (see above), and a write refuses a name Anki would not store, listing the name each file should have. In both cases the references to the old names need the same rename. Call What it changes Package.replace_media_references(renames) every reference to a renamed file: note fields, and names beginning with _ in notetype CSS and templates Package.read_apkg(..., repair_media_references=True) applies the renames the read made before returning, instead of warning Note.replace_media_references(renames) , Notetype.replace_underscored_css_imports(renames) , Template.replace_underscored_references(renames) the same rename for one note, stylesheet or template Package.trim_unused_media() drops every file nothing references, like Anki's Tools > Check Media A read that stores a file under a new name prints the renames as a map that replace_media_references() can take: pkg = Package.read_apkg("shared.apkg", keep_source_media=True) # Genanki2Warning: MediaEntries: media map contains filenames that Anki would not # store. [...] Pass this mapping to `genanki2.Package.replace_media_references()`: # { # 'casa?.mp3': 'casa.mp3', # } pkg.replace_media_references({"casa?.mp3": "casa.mp3"}) repair_media_references=True makes the same call during the read, without the warning: pkg = Package.read_apkg( "shared.apkg", keep_source_media=True, repair_media_references=True ) Cards and notes Call What it changes Anki equivalent is edited Collection.remove_empty_cards(keep_notes=False) removes the cards that a note no longer renders, with their reviews, and a note whose cards are all empty unless keep_notes=True Tools > Empty presets Call What it changes Anki equivalent Collection.collect_default_deck() adds the builtin DEFAULT_DECK when no deck has id 1 none: Anki cannot study a collection without it template when it creates one Notetype.repair_sort_field_idx() clamps a sort field index past the last field to the last field the same clamp on save Template.repair_target_deck_id() clears a deck docs.text: Settings genanki2 has four settings, each turned on and off by a pair of context managers: Setting Off On Affects Checks checks_disabled() checks_enabled() writing Warnings warnings_disabled() warnings_enabled() writing Database check repairs dbcheck_repairs_disabled() dbcheck_repairs_enabled() reading, assignment, writing Timestamping timestamping_disabled() timestamping_enabled() writing All four are on by default. At the end of the with block, the setting returns to its previous state. The *_enabled() methods turn a setting back on inside a block that turned it off: from genanki2 import Package, warnings_disabled, warnings_enabled pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) with warnings_disabled(): pkg.write_apkg("quiet.apkg") with warnings_enabled(): pkg.write_apkg("loud.apkg") examples/settings.py shows each one. Checks A check raises Genanki2Error for something that Anki would reject or quietly change, or that would break later, when reviewing cards. The checks run when a model is written or when called manually. See Checks and warnings for details on how they work and a complete list. A shared package that someone else made can hold values that Anki accepts, but genanki2's checks refuse, which would stop you from writing it back. checks_disabled() skips the checks during a write. An explicit pkg.check() still runs inside the block, so you can report a problem and then write anyway: from genanki2 import Genanki2Error, Package, checks_disabled pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) try: pkg.check() except Genanki2Error as error: print(f"Writing anyway: {error}") with checks_disabled(): pkg.write_apkg("copy.apkg") Warnings A warning ( Genanki2Warning ) points at something that Anki accepts but that is probably a mistake. The warnings run when a model is written, after the checks, or when called manually. See Checks and warnings for details on how they work and a complete list. warnings_disabled() skips the warnings during a write: they are not computed at all. An explicit pkg.warn() still warns inside the block. Python's warnings module works on them as on any other warning. A filter computes each warning and then discards it, so it is slower than warnings_disabled() , but it can pick warnings by message or turn them into errors: import warnings from genanki2 import Genanki2Warning warnings.simplefilter("error", Genanki2Warning) # every warning raises The context manager does not affect warnings raised during a read; filter them with the warnings module. Database check repairs Anki keeps some values as they are until the user runs Check Database, which then repairs them. genanki2 makes these repairs itself, so the package already holds what Anki would repair to, and warns about each value it changes. Repairs lists them. The repairs run when a package is read or written and when an attribute is assigned. dbcheck_repairs_disabled() keeps the values as they are, so the block has to wrap the read, the write and any assignment in between to disable the repairs completely. A model whose repairs run on assignment repairs itself again when it is assigned to outside the block. A repair method called explicitly still repairs. A write warns about each value kept, unless it runs inside warnings_disabled() . The checks are not affected. Timestamping Anki's import updates a note or a notetype that a user already has only when the incoming one has a newer modification time. So when a note or a notetype read from a package has changed, the write sets its modification time to the current time, as Anki does when it saves an edit. A modification time that you set yourself is kept. Freezing a model ( freeze() ) also sets it, following the setting at the time of the freeze. timestamping_disabled() keeps the time that was read, so an import leaves the copy that a user already has unchanged. A write warns about each change that an import would skip, unless it runs inside warnings_disabled() . An explicit update_modification_time() still sets the time. See Updating a package for what an import does with each change. Writing a package back as it was read With the checks, the warnings and the repairs disabled, the rows written are the rows read: nothing repaired, nothing refused (although a read can still refuse values in the wrong value range). The repairs run while reading, so the read has to be inside the block too: from genanki2 import ( Package, checks_disabled, dbcheck_repairs_disabled, warnings_disabled, ) with dbcheck_repairs_disabled(), checks_disabled(), warnings_disabled(): pkg = Package.read_apkg("shared.apkg", keep_source_media=True) pkg.write_apkg("copy.apkg")
