docs.text: Updating a package Read the package, change it, and write a new version. No need to hardcode ids: the identifiers come back out of the file, so the new version updates the notes that users already have. The examples on this page start from the package that Building a deck writes: from genanki2 import Package, guid_for, note pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) collection = pkg.collection word = collection.get_notetype(name="Italian word") vocabulary = collection.get_deck(name="Italian::Vocabulary") casa = collection.get_note(guid=guid_for(word.id, "casa")) Changing notes Notes override the subscript operator [] , which allows editing field values using their name: casa["English"] = "house, home" genanki2 keeps track of modifications applied to notes in order to update the modification time during the write process. Anki imports a note only when the incoming note's modification time is more recent than the one in the collection. The following snippet illustrates how this works by updating the time manually: print(casa.modification_time_s) casa["English"] = "house, home" casa.update_modification_time() print(casa.modification_time_s) An unchanged note keeps the time it was read with, so a user's own edit survives the import. A changed note replaces the user's copy, overwriting their edits. The same mechanism applies to a notetype whose template text, styling, or field and template names change. Changing which fields and templates it has is different, as the next section explains. The time has a resolution of one second, so a change written in the same second as the read, or as an earlier write that stamped the note, cannot be newer, and the write warns about it. A later write stamps it. A modification_time_s you set yourself is written as set. This mechanism can be disabled with the timestamping_disabled() context manager (see Timestamping ): from genanki2 import timestamping_disabled casa["English"] = "house, home" with timestamping_disabled(): pkg.write_apkg("italian-v2.apkg") Automatic timestamping is on by default and can be reenabled using the timestamping_enabled() context manager. Changing a notetype's fields or templates Once a notetype has shipped (your shared deck is imported by users), its lists of fields and templates are fixed. Adding, removing or reordering a field or a template makes the import add a second copy of the notetype. The notes that users already have stay on the old notetype and are not updated, and new notes go to the copy. Users can avoid this, by ticking "Merge note types" while importing, which is off by default. genanki2's write process warns when a notetype read from the package changed this way. Renaming a field or a template can be safe under certain circumstances: if they have been stamped with ids. None means they have no id. (Anki's import matches them by id and falls back to the name only when an id is missing.) for template in word.templates: print(template.name, template.config.id if template.config.id is not None else "None") When first building a package, it is highly recommended to call Notetype.fill_missing_ids() on each notetype to set ids on fields and templates. Call it only in the first build and read the package from that point on to make updates! Rebuilding the package generates random ids again. Leave it out (by commenting the call or putting it behind a flag) in a script that rebuilds an already shipped deck because later imports duplicate the notetype. parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() parser.add_argument( "--first-build", action="store_true", help="Give fields and templates ids." ) args = parser.parse_args() word = notetype(...) if args.first_build: word.fill_missing_ids() Adding notes New notes are added with collection.add_notes() and are studied after every card already in the deck: finestra = note(word, ["finestra", "window", ""], guid=guid_for(word.id, "finestra")) collection.add_notes([finestra], vocabulary) See Building a deck - add notes to the collection for details. Cards after an edit A card is not generated when a template's front side is empty. An edit (like adding a field value or editing the template itself) can make a template's front non-empty. Use collection.generate_missing_cards() to make the cards that notes did not produce before: pkg.media.append("audio/it_finestra.mp3") finestra["Audio"] = "[sound:it_finestra.mp3]" collection.generate_missing_cards() Filling a field is a change on a note read from a package, so the note is written with the current time and the import brings in the field along with the new card. Cards are not removed automatically if edits make a template's front empty (in Anki they stay until the user runs Tools > Empty Cards). Use collection.remove_empty_cards() to remove them from the package. finestra["Audio"] = "" collection.remove_empty_cards() Changing cards Anki's import never updates a card that a user already has: it skips them. Moving such a card to another deck, suspending, flagging or repositioning it reaches only users who import the card for the first time, and genanki2's write process warns about it. Changing decks and presets An import matches a deck by name (a renamed deck arrives as a new one, see Identifiers that keep a deck updatable ) and updates the deck that the user already has, whatever the modification times: its description, unless the incoming one is empty; its preset, when the user ticks "Import any deck presets" and the incoming deck does not use the default preset; the daily limits that the incoming deck sets, when the user ticks "Import any learning progress". from genanki2 import deck_config vocabulary.kind.description = "Common words and phrases." vocabulary.config = deck_config("Italian, slow", id=1_759_600_000_100, new_per_day=5) The import never changes a preset the user already has: a preset whose options changed reaches only users who do not have it yet (see Deck presets ). To ship new options, give the deck a new preset with an id of its own. Removing notes note_to_remove = collection.get_note(guid=guid_for(word.id, "mangiare")) collection.remove_notes([note_to_remove]) collection.remove_notes([...]) removes notes with their cards and reviews (unlike add_notes() , this method alters 3 collection lists: notes , cards and reviews ). An import never deletes anything, though: users who imported an earlier version keep the removed notes until they delete them themselves. Renaming media pkg.replace_media_references() renames a file wherever the collection refers to it: in note fields, and in a notetype's CSS and templates for names beginning with _ . The file on disk is not touched and the path in pkg.media is not updated: from pathlib import Path Path("audio/it_acqua.mp3").rename("audio/acqua.mp3") pkg.media.remove("audio/it_acqua.mp3") pkg.media.append("audio/acqua.mp3") pkg.replace_media_references({"it_acqua.mp3": "acqua.mp3"}) A package can hold a media name which Anki would not store. Reading it stores the file under a repaired name and emits a warning containing a map with renames to pass to this method. With repair_media_references=True , read_apkg() applies them itself. Media references lists the other calls that rename references. Writing the new version pkg.trim_unused_media() pkg.write_apkg("italian-v2.apkg") If using the read-update-write flow, use italian-v2.apkg for the next round of updates. examples/read_update_write.py illustrates the whole update seen here.

docs.text: Card generation An .apkg import doesn't generate cards, it brings in the cards that the package carries and nothing else. So genanki2 makes the cards Anki would make, when a note is added ( Collection.add_notes() ) and after an edit ( Collection.generate_missing_cards() ). Note.card_ordinals lists which cards a note gets. Which cards a note gets On a normal notetype, a template gives a card when its front renders (aka it's not empty). That means the front holds a plain field reference {{K}} to non-empty field K and every conditional around the reference is satisfied ( {{#C}} or {{^C}} ). You can check a template using Template.is_front_renderable() . Text outside a reference does not count towards determining if the template is empty or not. A field is considered empty if it holds only whitespace and line breaks. The special names count as filled for every note, except Tags , which needs the note to have tags, and FrontSide , which never does. A filter does not change the answer, so {{text:F}} renders when F is filled. On a cloze notetype, each cloze number gives a card, from any field. {{c1::…}} is card 0, {{c1,2::…}} gives cards 0 and 1. A cloze nested in another cloze counts too. c0 does not produce any cards. Every number from 500 up shares card 499: Anki gives each of them its own card 499 and removes all but one at the next "Check Database", so genanki2 makes one. All cards use the first template. A note with no card gets card 0, with a warning. Anki does the same. Note.card_ordinals reports the renderable cards, but it can be empty. Both add_notes() and generate_missing_cards() apply the fallback. Existing cards stay when their front becomes empty. Anki keeps them until the user runs "Empty Cards". An edit made to the note's values or to the template may make the front unrenderable. Collection.remove_empty_cards() removes them, for a package that should not hand those cards to new users. The two cloze warnings on Note , for cloze markup on a normal notetype and in a field for which the front does not pass through cloze: , read nested clozes the same way. docs.text: Collection schema v18 The Anki collection is a single SQLite database. The DDL is in src/genanki2/_schema.py , dumped from a collection the official client created. Everything here was read from Anki's Rust source ( rslib/ ) and from a freshly created collection. Quick guide 12 tables in 4 groups: Types. notetypes plus its fields and templates define the shape of a note: how many fields, what they are called, and the HTML templates that turns them into cards. A note points at a notetype by mid , and its field values are stored positionally, so field order is part of the contract. Content. notes holds the data necessary to produce a card using a notetype. One note produces one card per template whose condition its fields satisfy, so a two-way vocabulary note (i.e. a notetype with 2 templates) produces two cards from one row of text. cards holds what you review and carry all the scheduling state. Organisation. A deck is a group of cards. decks , although a flat table, fakes a tree through :: in the name. deck_config holds scheduling presets, which decks reference by id, so many decks can share one preset. config is a collection-wide key/value store. tags is a registry of known tags, separate from the tags actually written on each note. History and sync. revlog is an append-only log of answers and references cards . graves records deletions so a sync can replay them. col is a single row of collection metadata. Three special things: No foreign keys. cards.nid , notes.mid , cards.did and the rest are plain integers. SQLite enforces nothing; Anki maintains referential integrity in application code and repairs it in Check Database. A row pointing at a missing parent is writable and will be dealt with on import, not rejected. Config columns are serialized blobs. decks.common , decks.kind , notetypes.config , fields.config , templates.config and deck_config.config hold protobuf messages defined in anki/proto/anki/ . This is what makes the schema opaque to plain SQL and is the reason any collection writer needs the generated protobuf modules to write anything beyond a stock notetype. config.val is the exception because it is JSON, not protobuf (reference: rslib/src/storage/config/mod.rs ). Two id conventions. Row ids for notes , cards and revlog are the current time in milliseconds. When a row already holds that id, the insert uses max(id) + 1 instead, so adding many notes within one millisecond gives consecutive ids rather than a failure ( rslib/src/storage/note/add.sql ). Ids for decks , notetypes and deck_config are also timestamps at creation, but are treated as opaque stable identifiers afterwards: they are what an .apkg matches on when re-importing, so changing one forks the deck or notetype instead of updating it. Nothing enforces either convention; both are just what Anki happens to write. erDiagram notetypes ||--|{ fields : "fields.ntid" notetypes ||--|{ templates : "templates.ntid" notetypes ||--o{ notes : "notes.mid" notes ||--|{ cards : "cards.nid" decks ||--o{ cards : "cards.did" deck_config ||--o{ decks : "kind.normal.config_id" cards ||--o{ revlog : "revlog.cid" The remaining four tables join to nothing, so they are left out of the diagram: Table Key Holds Why it stands alone col id , always 1 Collection metadata: schema version, creation time, sync state. A singleton. Everything else in the collection is implicitly "the" collection's. config key Collection-wide settings, one row per setting. Keys are opaque strings, not references. tags tag The set of tags that exist, with their sidebar state. A registry mirroring what is written in notes.tags ; no row points at a note. graves (oid, type) Tombstones for deleted cards, notes and decks. oid names a row that was deleted, which says nothing about whether the id is in use now. unicase collation Six columns are declared COLLATE unicase : the name of decks, presets, notetypes, fields and templates, and tags.tag . The collation is Anki's own, registered from Rust, and stdlib sqlite3 refuses DDL that names a collation it does not know, so genanki2 registers one under the same name before running the DDL. The file stores only the name, and Anki resolves it against its own implementation when it opens the file. The comparator has to order strings as Anki's does: SQLite orders index entries physically by it, and a disagreement makes Anki's lookups through those indexes miss rows. str.casefold agrees with Anki's unicase 2.6.0 on every pair of the corpus in tests/test_unicase_matches_anki.py , while str.lower splits ß from ss and final sigma from medial sigma. Anki pins the crate to that exact version for the same reason, so a change of the pin is the signal to run the test again. COLLATE NOCASE is no substitute, since it folds ASCII only and breaks every non-ASCII deck name and tag. col One row, id = 1 , holding collection-wide metadata. Column Type Role id integer Always 1 . crt integer Creation time, seconds. Rounded back to the day's rollover hour (4am local by default), so it is a day boundary, not the exact moment of creation. Review cards count their due in days from this instant, which makes it the epoch of the whole scheduler. mod integer Last modification, milliseconds. scm integer Schema modification time, milliseconds. A client whose scm differs from the server's must do a full sync rather than an incremental one. ver integer Schema version, 18 . dty integer Dirty flag, unused in practice, 0 . usn integer Update sequence number for the collection, 0 in a fresh collection. ls integer Last sync time, milliseconds, 0 if never synced. conf text Legacy v11 global config JSON. Emptied by the upgrade to v18, now '' . models text Legacy v11 notetype JSON. Now '' . decks text Legacy v11 deck JSON. Now '' . dconf text Legacy v11 deck config JSON. Now '' . tags text Legacy v11 tag JSON. Now '' . The five legacy text columns are the visible seam between v11 and v18: the upgrade moved their contents into the normalized tables and blanked them, but did not drop the columns. They are NOT NULL , so a writer must supply '' . No indexes beyond the primary key. notes The text of a note, plus derived values that support search and duplicate detection. Column Type Role id integer Millisecond timestamp, primary key. guid text Random base91 string, ten characters. Identity across collections: the importer matches an incoming note to an existing one by guid , never by id . mid integer Notetype id. Determines how flds is interpreted. mod integer Last modification, seconds. usn integer Update sequence number, -1 until synced. tags text Space separated, with a leading and trailing space when non-empty ( vocab verb ), and exactly '' when empty ( rslib/src/tags/mod.rs:46 ). The padding is what makes tags LIKE '% vocab %' a correct whole-tag search. flds text All field values joined by \x1f (unit separator). Positional: field 0 is the notetype's field with ord = 0 . sfld integer The sort field's value, HTML stripped. Which field that is comes from the notetype's sort_field_idx . Declared integer deliberately so that numeric content sorts numerically under SQLite's type affinity, while text content stays text. csum integer First four bytes of the SHA-1 of the HTML-stripped first field, big-endian ( rslib/src/notes/mod.rs:320 ). A writer that sets them inconsistently produces a collection that works but sorts or deduplicates wrongly, and nothing reports it. cards One row per card. Every scheduling decision lives here. Column Type Role id integer Millisecond timestamp, primary key. nid integer Note id. did integer Deck id. ord integer Which template produced this card, matching templates.ord . For cloze notetypes it is the cloze number minus one instead. mod integer Last modification, seconds. usn integer Update sequence number, -1 until synced. type integer 0 new, 1 learning, 2 review, 3 relearning ( rslib/src/card/mod.rs:39 ). queue integer Where the scheduler will look for it: 0 new, 1 learning, 2 review, 3 day learning, 4 preview repeat, -1 suspended, -2 buried by the scheduler, -3 buried by the user. due integer Meaning depends on queue : a position in the new queue for 0 , a Unix timestamp in seconds for 1 and 4 , days since col.crt for 2 and 3 . ivl integer Current interval in days. 0 for a new card. factor integer Ease factor in permille, 2500 meaning 250%. 0 for a new card. reps integer Number of times answered. lapses integer Number of times a review card was failed. left integer Learning steps remaining, encoded as steps_today * 1000 + steps_total . 0 outside learning. odue integer The due value to restore when the card leaves a filtered deck. 0 otherwise. odid integer The deck to return to when the card leaves a filtered deck. 0 otherwise. flags integer User-visible colour flag, low bits of a u8. 0 for none. data text JSON object of optional extras: pos (original new-queue position), s / d / dr (FSRS stability, difficulty, desired retention), decay , lrt (last review time), cd (custom scheduling data). A new, never-studied card is type = 0, queue = 0, ivl = 0, factor = 0, reps = 0, lapses = 0, left = 0, odue = 0, odid = 0, flags = 0, data = '{}' , with due set to the next position from the nextPos config key. notetypes Column Type Role id integer Primary key, a timestamp at creation, stable thereafter. name text COLLATE unicase , unique. mtime_secs integer Last modification, seconds. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. config blob NotetypeConfig protobuf: CSS, LaTeX preamble and postamble, sort_field_idx , kind (normal or cloze), and the per-template field requirements Anki uses to decide which cards a note generates. idx_notetypes_name unique on (name) : notetype names are an enforced unique key, unlike deck names being unique only by the same kind of index. idx_notetypes_usn on (usn) . A fresh collection ships six: Basic, Basic (and reversed card), Basic (optional reversed card), Basic (type in the answer), Cloze, Image Occlusion. fields Column Type Role ntid integer Notetype id, half of the primary key. ord integer Position, from 0 . The index into notes.flds . name text COLLATE unicase . The name templates reference as {{Front}} . config blob FieldConfig protobuf: font, size, right-to-left, sticky, plain text, collapsed, excluded from search. WITHOUT ROWID , primary key (ntid, ord) . idx_fields_name_ntid unique on (name, ntid) : field names are unique within a notetype, which is what lets a template reference a field by name. templates Column Type Role ntid integer Notetype id, half of the primary key. ord integer Position, from 0 . Matches cards.ord . name text COLLATE unicase . Shown as the card type name. mtime_secs integer Last modification, seconds. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. config blob CardTemplateConfig protobuf: q_format and a_format (the question and answer HTML), their browser variants, target deck override, browser font ( anki/proto/anki/notetypes.proto:104 ). WITHOUT ROWID , primary key (ntid, ord) . idx_templates_name_ntid unique on (name, ntid) . idx_templates_usn on (usn) . The card HTML being inside a protobuf blob is the single most consequential fact in this schema for a writer: no custom card template can be produced by manipulating plain columns. decks Column Type Role id integer Primary key. 1 is always the Default deck. name text COLLATE unicase , unique. Hierarchy is encoded in the name with :: , so Italian::Verbs is a child of Italian . The parent must exist as its own row. mtime_secs integer Last modification, seconds. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. common blob DeckCommon protobuf: study counts, collapsed state, last studied, description flags. kind blob DeckKind protobuf, a oneof. Normal decks carry the deck_config id they use plus per-deck limit overrides and the description; filtered decks carry search terms, order and reschedule settings instead. idx_decks_name unique on (name) , under unicase , so Italian and italian collide. The hierarchy being string-encoded means a subdeck costs nothing structurally: write both rows, name the child with :: , and Anki renders the tree. deck_config Column Type Role id integer Primary key. 1 is always the Default preset. name text COLLATE unicase . mtime_secs integer Last modification, seconds. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. config blob DeckConfigInner protobuf: learning and relearning steps, new and review daily limits, starting ease, interval modifiers, leech threshold and action, burying options, FSRS parameters. No indexes beyond the primary key. Presets are few and looked up by id. config Collection-wide key/value settings. Column Type Role key text Primary key. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. mtime_secs integer Last modification, seconds. val blob JSON , not protobuf ( rslib/src/storage/config/mod.rs , serde_json::from_slice ). A boolean is the three bytes true , a string is quoted, so sortType is stored as "noteFld" with the quotes. WITHOUT ROWID . No secondary indexes. Column Type Role tag text Primary key, COLLATE unicase . :: marks hierarchy, as with decks. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. collapsed boolean Whether the sidebar shows it collapsed. config blob Nullable, the only nullable column in the schema. WITHOUT ROWID . No secondary indexes. The authoritative tags for a note are in notes.tags ; this table exists so the browser sidebar can list and collapse tags without scanning every note. A fresh collection has zero rows. An apkg export never writes this table, and an import rebuilds the registry from the notes it adds, so the collapsed state survives only in a colpkg. The export also strips marked and leech from every note, case-insensitively, so a note's tags can differ between a collection and a package exported from it, while the registry may still hold both. revlog Append-only log of answers, one row per button press. Drives the statistics screens and trains FSRS. Column Type Role id integer Millisecond timestamp of the review, primary key. cid integer Card id. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. ease integer Button pressed, 1 to 4 . 0 means a manual reschedule. ivl integer New interval. Positive is days, negative is seconds. lastIvl integer Previous interval, same sign convention. factor integer Ease after answering, permille. Under FSRS this holds normalized difficulty in the 100 to 1100 range instead. time integer Milliseconds spent answering. type integer 0 learning, 1 review, 2 relearning, 3 filtered, 4 manual, 5 rescheduled ( rslib/src/revlog/mod.rs:65 ). ix_revlog_cid on (cid) : a card's history. ix_revlog_usn on (usn) . An apkg carries the revlog only when exported with scheduling, and an import reads it only with with_scheduling on. An imported entry has its cid rewritten to the id its card was given, and one whose id the target already holds is dropped rather than renumbered. Deleting a card does not delete its reviews, so a row whose cid names no card is an ordinary state of a real collection. graves Deletion tombstones, so a sync can tell "deleted here" from "not yet created here". Column Type Role oid integer The deleted row's id, half of the primary key. type integer 0 card, 1 note, 2 deck ( rslib/src/storage/graves/mod.rs:15 ). usn integer Update sequence number. -1 while the deletion is still pending upload. Only sync reads this table. An apkg export never writes it, so a colpkg is the only package that carries graves. They are SQLite's query planner statistics, produced by ANALYZE , which Anki runs as part of vacuum; reindex; analyze when the schema is marked modified ( rslib/src/storage/sqlite.rs:643 ). SQLite creates and populates them itself; a writer should leave them out and let the client generate them. What varies between two fresh collections Creating an empty collection twice does not give the same bytes. Everything that moves, measured by diffing three empty collections cell by cell (two created moments apart, one under a different timezone): Where Example What it is col.crt 1785895200 Day zero of the scheduler. Changes with the creation date and with the timezone. col.scm 1785934748825 Schema modification time, milliseconds. config row creationOffset , val -120 UTC offset in minutes at creation. Changes with the timezone, not with time. config row curModel , val 1785934748830 The Basic notetype's id, as a bare JSON number. Follows the notetype ids below. config row curModel , mtime_secs 1785934748 Seconds timestamp. The only config row a fresh collection leaves with a non-zero usn or mtime_secs . notetypes.id , and fields.ntid / templates.ntid referencing it 1785934748830 through ...835 The six stock notetype ids: millisecond timestamps, allocated consecutively as the notetypes are added. fields.config blob, field 9 trailing 48 <varint> The field's stable id, rand::random() ( rslib/src/notetype/fields.rs:41 ). templates.config blob, field 8 trailing 40 <varint> The template's stable id, rand::random() ( rslib/src/notetype/templates.rs:96 ). The two random ids exist for merging notetypes on import (Anki 23.10 and later), so they identify a field or template across installations rather than describing its content. They are full-range int64 and negative about half the time, which is why an otherwise identical fields.config blob is 19 bytes in one collection and 20 in the next: a negative value costs a 10-byte varint. Everything else is stable: notetypes.config (it carries original_stock_kind , not an id), all of deck_config , all of decks , col.mod at 0 , every remaining config row at usn = 0, mtime_secs = 0 , and the five legacy text columns in col at '' . Row order is stable without an ORDER BY . The rowid tables scan in rowid order, and the WITHOUT ROWID tables scan in primary key order, which is (ntid, ord) for fields and templates and the key string for config .

docs.text: One row per card. Every scheduling decision lives here. docs.text: A registry of tags that exist, distinct from the tags recorded on notes. Column Type Role tag text Primary key, COLLATE unicase . :: marks hierarchy, as with decks. usn integer Update sequence number, sync marker. collapsed boolean Whether the sidebar shows it collapsed. config blob Nullable, the only nullable column in the schema. docs.text: Creating an empty collection twice does not give the same bytes. Everything that moves, measured by diffing three empty collections cell by cell (two created moments apart, one under a different timezone): Where Example What it is col.crt 1785895200 Day zero of the scheduler. Changes with the creation date and with the timezone. col.scm 1785934748825 Schema modification time, milliseconds. config row creationOffset , val -120 UTC offset in minutes at creation. Changes with the timezone, not with time. config row curModel , val 1785934748830 The Basic notetype's id, as a bare JSON number. Follows the notetype ids below. config row curModel , mtime_secs 1785934748 Seconds timestamp. The only config row a fresh collection leaves with a non-zero usn or mtime_secs . notetypes.id , and fields.ntid / templates.ntid referencing it 1785934748830 through ...835 The six stock notetype ids: millisecond timestamps, allocated consecutively as the notetypes are added. fields.config blob, field 9 trailing 48 <varint> The field's stable id, rand::random() ( rslib/src/notetype/fields.rs:41 ). templates.config blob, field 8 trailing 40 <varint> The template's stable id, rand::random() ( rslib/src/notetype/templates.rs:96 ). The two random ids exist for merging notetypes on import (Anki 23.10 and later), so they identify a field or template across installations rather than describing its content. They are full-range int64 and negative about half the time, which is why an otherwise identical fields.config blob is 19 bytes in one collection and 20 in the next: a negative value costs a 10-byte varint. Everything else is stable: notetypes.config (it carries original_stock_kind , not an id), all of deck_config , all of decks , col.mod at 0 , every remaining config row at usn = 0, mtime_secs = 0 , and the five legacy text columns in col at '' . Row order is stable without an ORDER BY . The rowid tables scan in rowid order, and the WITHOUT ROWID tables scan in primary key order, which is (ntid, ord) for fields and templates and the key string for config .

docs.text: Frozen models: limitations and possible solutions Every genanki2 model inherits freeze() from DeepFreezable ( src/genanki2/freezable.py ). A frozen model: refuses assigning or deleting a public attribute replaces its lists, dicts and sets with tuples, frozendict s and frozenset s freezes every model it holds The builtin constants are frozen where builtins.py builds them. Behaviour below was measured on pydantic 2.13.4. Writes that go around the guard The guard sits in __setattr__ and __delattr__ , so anything that writes the instance __dict__ directly passes it. For example, pydantic.BaseModel.model_copy(update=...) does that on the copy it returns, or any instance.__dict__[name] = value assignment. The freeze protects against accidental writes, but it is not a security boundary. For the builtin notetypes, the one value a writer has reason to set, the modification time, is checked again at write time by Package.check_builtin_notetype_versions() . BaseModel.model_copy() also copies the flag, so a copy of a frozen model is frozen. builtin_notetype() , default_deck() and default_deck_config() build a new, writable model instead of copying. A frozen model is not equal to its unfrozen twin [a] == (a,) is False in Python, so once deepfreeze() has swapped a list for a tuple, a frozen model compares unequal to an unfrozen one, even if they hold the same values. To compare content and not structure, DeepFreezable has is_content_equivalent() : it compares sequences item by item, mappings by keys and values, pydantic models of the same class by their fields, other Freezable instances of the same class by their public attributes, and anything else with == . It is symmetric, and Collection uses it when two models share an id. Dumping a frozen model BaseModel.model_dump() on a frozen model warns ( PydanticSerializationUnexpectedValue ) for every field annotated as a list that now holds a tuple. A dict field holding a frozendict makes model_dump(mode="json") raise PydanticSerializationError . What genanki2 writes does not go through either path. A config blob reaches its row through ProtobufModel.to_bytes() , which reads each attribute and hands it to protobuf, and protobuf accepts a tuple as it accepts a list. Notetype.fields and templates are excluded from the dump, Note builds its row itself, and no model has a dict field. The warning appears only when a caller dumps a frozen model directly. Possible solutions, if a direct dump of a frozen model has to be clean: A field serializer per list field, returning a list. The cost is limited to those fields, and each new list field needs its own. A wildcard wrap serializer in a mixin placed before pydantic.BaseModel , field_serializer("*", mode="wrap", check_fields=False) , that turns tuples back into lists and frozendict s into dicts before calling the handler. It covers every field at once, but it cannot tell a tuple deepfreeze() made from a field annotated as a tuple, and it turns the latter into a list, which moves the warning to that field. The same wildcard serializer, passing the value through pydantic.TypeAdapter(annotation).validate_python() with the field's annotation before calling the handler. Validation converts each container to what the annotation declares, at any depth, so tuple fields stay tuples. The price is a validation pass on every field of every dump, and validators inside the annotation run again. The TypeAdapter has to be cached per annotation. A JSON dump fails on any model holding a config blob, frozen or not: the blob serializes to bytes, which pydantic encodes as UTF-8. ser_json_bytes="base64" in CheckedModel.model_config makes it a base64 string. A wrap serializer that returns to_bytes() in Python mode and hands the nested model to the handler in JSON mode gives readable JSON instead, at every blob field, and brings the frozen-list warning into JSON mode with it. What deepfreeze() loses or leaves alone Conversion keeps values and drops behaviour: a defaultdict stops supplying defaults, a Counter stops returning 0 for a missing key, a ChainMap is flattened, and an array.array becomes a tuple of numbers. A tuple subclass other than a namedtuple is left as it is, since nothing says how to rebuild it, and so is a dict view, which stays tied to its dict. A container referenced from two places becomes two separate copies. The buffer under a read-only memoryview still changes when written through another reference. Private attributes The guard leaves names beginning with _ writable, and is_content_equivalent() does not compare them, but freeze() walks the whole __dict__ . On a Freezable that is not a pydantic model, a list in a private attribute becomes a tuple and the models in it are frozen, while the attribute itself can still be reassigned. A pydantic model keeps private attributes in __pydantic_private__ and extra attributes in __pydantic_extra__ , so the freeze reaches neither: an extra attribute cannot be reassigned but a list it holds stays a list. Walking only the public attributes would make the freeze agree with the guard and the comparison. Cycles and iterators The frozen flag is set after the held models are frozen, so two models holding each other raise RecursionError , and so does a container that holds itself. Setting the flag before the walk would make cycles safe, but a failure halfway would then leave a model marked frozen over held models the walk never reached. An iterator or generator stored in an attribute is consumed by the search. genanki2's models don't hold these.

docs.text: Model shapes Why the pydantic models under src/genanki2/models/ hold what they hold. SQLite rows An SQLite row becomes a model through cls.model_validate(row) , with each field aliased to its column. Defaults, ignored extra columns such as ntid , and error messages that name the column all come from pydantic. The alternative, a hand-written mapping per model, would spell every default twice. Notetypes Ordinals are list positions A field's or template's ordinal is its position in the notetype's list, and nothing else. Field.to_row(notetype_id, ordinal) takes one, to_rows() supplies it from enumerate , and from_rows() sorts by the ord column and then forgets it. Anki derives ordinals the same way when it saves a notetype's fields and templates ( update_notetype_fields , update_notetype_templates ). An ordinal attribute would store the same fact twice, and reverse() on the list would make them disagree without firing any validator, validate_assignment included. One notetype, three tables A notetype spans the notetypes , fields and templates tables. That is why from_rows() and to_rows() exist next to from_row() and to_row() : they are the only place that knows the three tables must agree on the notetype id and on the ordinals. Duplicate and empty lists raise Two fields or two templates with the same name raise. Both tables have a unique index on the name, so a duplicate would otherwise surface as a bare IntegrityError naming neither the field nor the notetype. Renaming the duplicate is no fix: Anki's own repair adds a + suffix, which breaks every {{Front}} the user wrote in the templates. An empty fields or templates list raises. Without a template, a note gets no cards. Without a field, flds , sfld and csum mean nothing. There is no partial result worth writing. field_values() is a notetype method Notetype.field_values(mapping) builds a note's field list from a dict. It cannot be a Note validator: pydantic builds __init__ from the annotation, so passing a mapping to fields: list[str] is a type error at the call site, and a before-validator sees notetype before it is validated. A Note classmethod would have to redeclare every other Note field. field_index() and field_names already live on the notetype. Notes Random guids by default Without guid= , a note gets random bits. Stability is opt-in, through guid_for(notetype_id, *key) . A random default says what is true of a note with no identity of its own: it is a new note, and a rebuild adds it rather than pretending to update something. The other common default, a hash of the note's fields, mints a new guid at every edit, so the note forks on import instead of updating, and two notes with equal fields under different notetypes collide. guid_for() takes the identity from the caller instead, from whatever names the row in the source data, and mixes in the notetype id. Decks and presets Deck names use :: Deck holds the human name, with :: between components, and converts it at the row boundary. Anki stores \x1f in its place, and native_deck_name is not idempotent, since \x1f is an ASCII control character that the normalization strips: a subdeck read back and rewritten would collapse Test\x1fNested into TestNested . A deck's preset is an object and an id The row holds only the id ( kind.config_id ), so the object cannot be required. An id alone is what a caller reading a package back gets, and dropping the id would make writing one impossible. Keeping both lets Deck.config be collected into Collection.deck_configs while the id still stands on its own. The cost is two places that can disagree. sync_normal_kind_config_id copies the object's id into the blob on every validation, and check_normal_kind_config_id refuses a pair that still disagrees at write time, since Anki reads the blob and would schedule the deck by whatever id it holds. Presets are matched by id, not by name deck_config.name compares case-insensitively like deck and notetype names, but it has no unique index and the importer never compares it. Two presets may share a name, so check_unique_names covers decks and notetypes only. The id does not guarantee much either. The importer imports presets only when the user ticks "Import any deck presets" ( with_deck_configs , off by default). It then adds an incoming preset only when the user has none with that id ( add_deck_config_if_unique_undoable ), never updates one, and keeps the id as it is, unlike deck, note and notetype ids, which it remaps. So a deck has to be usable on preset 1, and shipping a preset is a request rather than a guarantee. Shipping preset 1 never changes an existing deck's scheduling, since a deck moves to the incoming preset only when that preset is not 1. An export carries only the presets its decks name, and an export without scheduling empties their FSRS parameters (see Changing decks and presets ). Cards A card's original deck is an id or a deck odid is the one reference in the library allowed to dangle. A package exported with scheduling can name an original deck that no longer exists; Anki's exporter documents this, and answering the card treats the deck as not found. So the field is a union of an id and a Deck : A Deck -only field would force from_row() to invent a deck, or to refuse a row that Anki opens without complaint. An int -only field would make a caller who builds a card in a filtered deck remember to append the home deck to the collection. A Deck object is collected into Collection.decks like every other reference. The union has two costs. No use site can assume the deck is there, and the unresolved id is what real collections produce. A caller also has two ways to write the same card, and every check accepts both. original_deck_id is what the rest of the library reads and what to_row() writes. The bound sits on the int arm, Annotated[Annotated[int, UInt63] | Deck, ...] . A constraint on the whole union raises TypeError from pydantic's constraint machinery when a Deck arrives, instead of the ValidationError a caller catches with everything else. last_review_time is passed through A last_review_time that disagrees with the revlog is not checked, by either CardData or Collection : Anki's only repair for it is in the database check ( fix_card_properties ), which no import calls, and it walks only cards that have revlog entries. An import without scheduling resets the card and clears its memory state, but leaves lrt in place. Without a memory state, the scheduler ignores the day count lrt feeds ( next_states ), and a card that keeps one overwrites lrt at its next answer. What is left is a package carrying both a revlog and a card that contradicts it, imported with scheduling. genanki2 can only have read such a package, not written it. Builtin notetypes Frozen constants and a customization function The constants such as BASIC_NOTETYPE are the frozen reference copies, and builtin_notetype() is the way to customize one. The constants are cached calls of the function, and the function reads the reference rows again on every call. Documenting the function as the entry point makes "change a builtin" mean "change an object nobody else holds", while the constants stay the shared, unmodified object a package points at. The freeze enforces it: assigning to a constant or changing a list it holds raises, and a copy made with model_copy() is frozen too, so the function is the only way to get a builtin that can change. BUILTIN_NOTETYPES is a tuple of the constants, for iterating or keying, not for changing. default_deck() , default_deck_config() , default_collection_metadata() and default_config_entries() follow the same shape for the stock deck, preset, col row and config entries, each reading the reference rows again on every call. Builtins ship with modification time 0 An import stores the incoming modification time as it is, and replaces a notetype the collection already holds only when the incoming one is newer. docs.text: Reading and collection packages The reasons behind how the reader and the two writers behave. What they do is in Reading a package . Reading a package The reader exists for read-update-write: read the package shipped last time, change what changed, write it back. So every decision below leans towards handing back what Anki wrote, and towards failing where it cannot, rather than guessing. The envelope names the entry, col.ver names the schema The meta entry, or the collection filename when there is none, decides three things: which zip entry holds the collection, whether it is compressed, and which media map format the package uses. It says nothing about the schema. So the reader opens the entry and refuses a col.ver other than 18. Anki accepts 11 through 18 and upgrades on open; genanki2 models one schema. Picking the entry by a name the reader recognises would go wrong: every package in the latest format also carries a schema 11 collection.anki2 stub beside collection.anki21b , holding one "please update Anki" note. A reader that took it would read a valid collection with the wrong contents. An exported apkg holds a minimal collection Anki builds a fresh collection for the package and inserts the exported rows into it. So the package carries the default config entries, deck 1 and preset 1, even when the export did not need them. Only crt and creationOffset are copied from the source. Read errors are raised outside validators PackageReadError and CollectionReadError (see Read errors ) are raised only from plain methods and classmethods. Pydantic wraps any ValueError a validator raises into a ValidationError , so raising them inside a validator would lose their type. Orphan rows are kept raw A field, template, note, card or revlog row whose parent is missing goes to the matching Collection.orphan_* list, and is written back unchanged. A model cannot be built without the object its row points at, and inventing that object or dropping the row would each alter what Anki wrote. Anki deletes such rows in Check Database, and an apkg never carries them because the exporter gathers rows by reference. A collection copied off disk can hold them, though, such as revlog rows whose card was deleted. A model that raises fails the whole read There is no lenient mode, for the same reason the models have no strictness setting . The recovery path is the database that extract_dir writes before parsing it. A deck naming a missing preset keeps the id Such a deck reads with config = None and keeps its preset id. Anki schedules it on preset 1 and never rewrites the id, so the reader invents no preset and repairs nothing. The write warns, and the repair is opt-in (see Decks and presets ). Ids in the future are reported, not renumbered An id more than a day in the future stays as read. Renumbering it would rewrite identifiers the round trip owes back, and would not spare the user anything: The merge importer renumbers such ids on its temporary copy of every package it reads, resolving any clash with the ids the user's collection already holds. A restore renumbers nothing. The rows keep their ids until the user runs the database check, which renumbers them the same way. A kept media source is checked before writing Package.media holds paths on disk, so a read has to give the media files a home (see Managing media files ). A kept source is checked before the destination zip is opened: It has to still exist. It has to hold every entry the read found. It has to declare the same envelope, since the envelope decides whether an entry is a file or a zstd frame of one. Its media entry has to be the one the read found, compared by the CRC-32. In the latest envelope the map holds each file's size and SHA-1, so a changed file changes the map. A legacy map holds only names, so a file replaced there under the same name is copied as it now stands. In the latest envelope the CRC covers the map's zstd frame, so a source rewritten with the same files but another compression level is refused too. The destination may not be the source itself, a hard link to it, or a spelling of it that a filesystem ignoring case resolves to the same file. The package would go on copying entries by a numbering the new file no longer has, and a file the new package drops would lose its only copy: pkg = Package.read_apkg("italian.apkg", keep_source_media=True) pkg.media.append("extra.txt") pkg.write_apkg("italian.apkg") # Correct write, but because of "extra.txt", # after the write the tracked media files data is # out-of-sync with the actual file on disk pkg.write_apkg("italian.apkg") # Second write reads the wrong bytes from the source Media names are repaired, references are not The read warns with the rename mapping instead of applying it (see Media references ), because applying it rewrites note fields, templates and CSS, which is data Anki wrote. The writer refuses a package whose references name a file it does not carry, so a caller who skips the step gets an error, not a broken deck. Anki handles the two envelopes differently: a name that is not normalized fails the whole import in the latest format, while in the legacy format it is normalized and the notes are rewritten to match. genanki2 repairs both alike on read, and leaves the strict half to the writer, where Package.check_media_paths() refuses any name that normalize_media_name() would change. Collection packages What a restore does and which file names each writer accepts are in Collection packages . Every media entry carries a SHA-1 A restore skips a file the media folder already holds, and decides that from the SHA-1 in the media entry. So write_colpkg() fills it on every entry. Each import is a class Package and CollectionPackage share their fields, media handling and envelope. They differ in the file name they accept and the checks they run. read_apkg() and read_colpkg() read the same files, since nothing inside a package tells the two apart. The class the caller reads into decides how the file is written back, so no flag says which import a file is for. Moving between the two is an explicit construction from the other's fields. File names are matched the way Anki's client does Both writers match a name case-sensitively, on the exact name, the prefix and the suffix, as Anki's desktop client does. How AnkiDroid routes a file has not been checked. Checks that differ between a merge and a restore The checks that a restore needs differ from a merge's wherever the verdict depends on what the importer does. Each writer passes the phases a SerializationContext naming its output, and the model that owns the data decides from it whether a finding is an error or a warning, and what the message says. Without a context nothing is skipped: a finding only a restore refuses is a warning, and the message names what happens under each import. Check Package CollectionPackage Why they differ Builtin notetype versions raises skipped A merge replaces a notetype only when the incoming one is newer, so a stamped builtin overwrites the user's copy. A restore replaces everything, and a user's collection can hold a builtin the user has since edited. Media references without a file raises warns Real collections carry them routinely (Anki's "Check Media" lists them), and writing back a backup must not fail on data the user already has. A restore removes no file, so the reference may still resolve. Ids in the future warns: Anki renumbers them on import warns: they stay until the database check The merge renumbers on its temporary copy. A restore keeps the ids, and the database check later renumbers them and moves the added dates and review times with them. schedVer other than 2 warns, when a card is out of the new queue raises A merge upgrades a package to v2 when any card is out of the new queue, which rewrites the review history. A restore upgrades nothing, so the collection opens on a scheduler Anki no longer runs, or not at all. No deck 1 silent raises A merge lands in a collection that has deck 1. A restored collection without it opens, but every scheduler call fails, and the database check does not recreate it. Collection.collect_default_deck() adds it.

docs.text: Repairs that alter what they read Wherever genanki2 interprets a value it reads (field-name repair, tag splitting, sfld and csum , the deck-name separator, media names), it has to leave what Anki wrote unchanged. Reading an untouched package and writing it back reproduces every row. Repairs are the exception. A repair that runs during validation runs on from_row() too, so a package holding a value it repairs does not come back as it went in. Repairs fall into three classes, which differ in whether a caller can switch them off. Mandatory repairs A mandatory repair changes a value that has no effect in Anki as it is: Bounded preset values. Anki substitutes the default for an out-of-range preset value as it reads the preset, so keeping the value keeps something inert. cards.due and cards.odue outside the 32-bit signed range, and revlog.time outside the 32-bit unsigned range. Anki reads 0 in their place as it loads the card or the review, and an apkg import stores what it loaded, so the user ends up with 0 whatever the package held. Normalized names and text. Anki makes the same change when it saves the value. notes.sfld and notes.csum . Both are mechanical derivations of the fields, which the caller chose to change. Note holds neither column: preserving what was read would mean carrying two values whose only purpose is to be written back, and deciding what they mean once fields is edited. Recomputing them reproduces what Anki stored for an unedited note. Opt-out repairs An opt-out repair changes a value that Anki repairs in the database check and nowhere else. Those values are live: a new card at position 3,000,000 stays at that position until the user runs Check Database by hand, through any number of exports and imports. The database check repairs the card values in one function ( fix_card_properties ) and the review durations in another ( fix_revlog_properties ), and the importer shifts due only for review and day-learning cards ( shift_collection_relative_dates ). genanki2 repairs them by default anyway. Turning a default repair into an opt-in later only stops rewriting data, while adding a repair later would start rewriting data that earlier releases preserved. dbcheck_repairs_disabled() turns them off as a set (see below ). docs.text: Validation How the pydantic models under src/genanki2/models/ decide whether they can be written, and when those decisions run. Permissive while building, strict at the write A model accepts an incomplete state while it is being built, so "construct empty, append later" works. Completeness is checked once, when the object claims to be finished: in to_rows() and the other entry points described below. The models have no strictness setting. The only way past the checks is checks_disabled() , which covers a whole write. Checks and warnings A write runs two named judgements on every model: check() raises: the write cannot proceed. warn() warns: Anki accepts the value, but does something the caller did not ask for. Keeping them apart lets a caller ask for either verdict without producing any rows, and turn the warnings off with warnings_disabled() while keeping the checks. Three base classes carry this machinery: CheckedModel holds pydantic's model_config that every model shares and the 3 phases. RowModel[R] adds from_row() and to_row() , and holds the library's single cast . Notetype is the exception that doesn't use from_row() and to_row() and adds its own from_rows() and to_rows() because it aggregates the fields and templates. ProtobufModel adds from_bytes() and to_bytes() . Phases, emitters and entry points Every method that serializes a model has one of three roles: Role Methods What it does Phase prepare() , check() , warn() changes or judges a model, and produces nothing Emitter _row() , _bytes() , CardData._json() , Collection._sqlite() , _PackageBase._write_*() produces output, and calls only other emitters Entry point to_row() , to_rows() , to_bytes() , to_json() , write_sqlite() , write_apkg() , write_colpkg() runs the phases over its own tree, then its emitter A parent reaches its children through their emitters, never through their entry points. So a write judges each model once, from the entry point the caller invoked, however deep the model sits. The whole tree is prepared before anything is checked, because a parent's checks read its children. Otherwise a collection would refuse a card for an original deck that the card's own repair is about to clear. Notetype.to_row() runs only its row-local checks, so that to_rows() stays the point where a notetype is checked as a whole. Why the phases are methods and not pydantic validators The checks have to run when a package is written, not only when a model is built. A model can change after its validators last ran: a list edited in place, such as notetype.templates.pop() , fires no validator. And a check that reads several objects, such as a card's template ordinal against its notetype's templates, can only be judged once all of them are in their final state. Pydantic validators cannot be made to run at that point. They run when a model is built and, with validate_assignment , when a field is assigned. Serializing a model runs no validator. The only way to make pydantic validate an existing model again is the revalidate_instances setting, which applies when a model is passed into a field of another model. It does not fit either way: With "never" , the default, the model is accepted as it is and nothing runs. With "always" , pydantic validates the model by building a new copy of it, and of every model it holds. A notetype shared by many notes would become one copy per note. An edit to the notetype in collection.notetypes would then no longer reach the notes, and the walk would judge every copy separately. So prepare() , check() and warn() are plain methods, and the entry points call them. What a write changes on the model The emitters change nothing. A write changes the models only in prepare() , in three places: TimestampedRowModel.prepare() sets the modification time of a note or notetype changed since it was last stamped. Collection.prepare() appends referenced objects to the collection's lists (see Referenced objects and the collection's lists ). Card.prepare() clears an original deck and due that the card's own deck no longer explains. Its validator makes the same repair, but a card cannot tell when its filtered deck turns normal. Each is idempotent: a second write with no edit in between writes the same rows. A model holds two kinds of state about the files around it, and only one of them follows a write: What the model was read from stays as the read left it: the fingerprint of the row, the modification time and id read, and a package's kept media source. Checks and warnings compare against it to report what changed since the read. What has been published follows the writes: the time a note or notetype was last stamped with, and the content it was stamped for. A later write compares against it, so an edit made after one write is stamped again by the next. A write that leaves the time where it was, in the same second as the last stamp or inside timestamping_disabled() , leaves this state too, and the next write stamps the edit. The published state lives on the model, not on the package or collection that wrote it. Anki compares an incoming note with the copy in the user's collection, and every package of a deck feeds that one collection, so a note written into two packages has one history. The second package carries the first one's stamp when the note is unchanged since, and a later one when it is not. A package written over its kept source is refused rather than followed for the same reason: the source is read state, describing the file the media is copied from (see A kept media source is checked before writing ). Walking the model tree A phase called with recursive=True runs on every model reachable from where it is called, each object once. The walk lives in CheckedModel . It follows every CheckedModel that a field holds, directly or inside a container, so a field added later is covered without a hand-written branch. To keep the walk cheap, it reads only the fields whose annotation could hold a model, decided once per class. The strings in Note.fields and the scalar columns are never walked. A test checks that reading every field would reach the same objects. The walk gathers the reachable models breadth first, telling objects apart by identity, and runs the phase on each with recursive=False . An override reads recursive=False as "apply only my own rules". The result: A check from a note covers its notetype. A check from a review covers its card, the card's note and decks, and the notetype. From a collection, a notetype that every note shares is judged and warned about once, not once per note. Some details follow from how the walk is built: The set of models already seen lives for one call. A phase run inside another, such as a to_bytes() inside a check, starts a walk of its own. A model is handed to the phase before its fields are read, so the walk follows what the phase leaves behind. A collection inside a package collects its references when it is prepared, and the models it collects are then prepared too. An equal copy of a model held somewhere else is a separate object, and is judged separately. collect_* refuses an unequal one at write time. Switching checks and warnings off checks_disabled() and warnings_disabled() turn off what a write runs automatically, so that a package Anki wrote can be written back even when it holds a value a genanki2 check rejects. checks_enabled() and warnings_enabled() turn them back on inside such a block (see Checks ). The switches are read at the entry point, never inside a phase, so an explicit check() or warn() inside the block still runs. Preparation runs whatever the switches say, since collecting fills the lists the writer writes from. Only the context managers are public, so a disabled state cannot outlive the block that set it. dbcheck_repairs_disabled() is the exception: its repairs run during validation, so the validators read it. See Switching the opt-out repairs off . Referenced objects and the collection's lists Models refer to each other as objects: a card holds its note and its deck, a note holds its notetype, etc. The collection also keeps flat lists ( notes , decks , etc.) and the writer writes rows from those lists only. Two things can go wrong between the references and the lists: An object is referenced but missing from its list. Its row would not be written, and the row referring to it would name an id that the file does not hold. Two different objects share one id. For example, a card's note and a note already in collection.notes have the same id but different fields or modification times. Only one row can be written for that id, and nothing says which one. Collecting handles both ( Collection.collect_references() , which the prepare phase of every write runs). It appends each referenced object that is missing from its list, and raises when the list already holds a different object under the same id. Collecting compares content, because it decides which object gets written. So a caller can append just the cards it builds: their notes, decks, notetypes and presets fill in by themselves. Collection.check_referential_integrity() asks a narrower question: does every note's notetype, every card's note and every card's deck have its id in the matching list? It compares ids only, because the file stores only ids, and Anki resolves a row whose id is in the file whatever the object behind it holds. A note held in two different versions therefore passes this check, and only collecting refuses it. In a write, collecting runs before any check, so the check finds the lists already filled. Calling Collection.check() without preparing first reports a reference that collecting would have added. Arguments of Field.to_row() and Template.to_row() A field or template row holds two values that the field or template does not own: the id of its notetype ( ntid ) and its position in the notetype's list ( ord ). So Field.to_row(notetype_id, ordinal) and Template.to_row(notetype_id, ordinal) take them as two plain ints and write them unchecked. The fields and templates tables declare no foreign key, so a wrong ntid would write rows that no notetype owns, without any error from SQLite. Every other value a write produces is checked: a model attribute by its annotation, and a row read with from_row() by model_validate . The two ints need no check of their own, because both come from the notetype. Notetype.to_rows() passes self.id , which Notetype already validates, and an ordinal from enumerate , which is 0, 1, 2… by construction. Validating the notetype's id covers the ntid of every row. What no validation can show is that to_rows() passes these values down correctly. Two tests check it: test_the_owning_id_comes_from_the_notetype changes the notetype's id and checks that every field and template row carries the new one. test_ordinals_follow_list_position reverses the list and checks that the ord values still run 0, 1, 2… in the new order. Checking the arguments as well would mean pydantic.validate_call on both methods. In lax mode it also turns "1" into 1 , so it would catch almost nothing the notetype does not already catch. Bounds that raise and bounds that repair How Anki reads a column decides what genanki2 does with a value out of range: Anki reads the column strictly: a value that does not fit makes the whole row unreadable, so the bound raises. A bound that raises refuses nothing Anki would open. Anki falls back to another value: Anki reads the fallback in place of what is stored, so every code path that loads the row sees the fallback, and an apkg import stores it. genanki2 repairs the value to the same fallback as it reads it, as a mandatory repair (see The repairs ). This covers the preset values under Bounded , Card.due and Card.original_due ( 0 outside the 32-bit signed range), and Review.time_ms ( 0 outside the 32-bit unsigned range). A value inside Anki's type can still be one that Anki's database check changes: a Card.template_ord above 30,000, or a Card.interval_days or Review.time_ms above 2**31 - 1 . Anki opens such a value as it is, so it is not a bound but an opt-out repair . Ids and times are bounded to values that make sense, even though Anki reads them as any 64-bit integer: an id is positive, and a time is 0 or later. Anki never writes anything else, and nothing in Anki gives a negative time or id a meaning. The cost is that genanki2 cannot read a collection holding such a value, so the bound is widened if one turns up in real data. Review.review_type is the one value read with a fallback that genanki2 keeps. Anki reads a review kind it does not know as a learning review, while the field is ReviewType | int and keeps the number. The fallback is what an older Anki makes of a kind a newer Anki added, and repairing it would erase the kind for the newer Anki too. usn is bounded only by its type, although Anki writes nothing below -1. A value below -1 makes an object count as already synced: a client sync sends the objects whose usn is -1, and the server those at or above the client's last count. Nothing genanki2 writes is held back by it, but only because of two Anki behaviours: an apkg import replaces every usn with the collection's own, and a colpkg restore forces a full sync, which uploads the whole file whatever each row's usn . If either changes, a value below -1 could keep an object from ever syncing, and the bound has to be reconsidered.
