docs.text: A model accepts an incomplete state while it is being built, so "construct empty, append later" works. Completeness is checked once, when the object claims to be finished: in to_rows() and the other entry points described below. The models have no strictness setting. The only way past the checks is checks_disabled() , which covers a whole write.
docs.title: Permissive while building, strict at the write

docs.text: A write runs two named judgements on every model: check() raises: the write cannot proceed. warn() warns: Anki accepts the value, but does something the caller did not ask for. Keeping them apart lets a caller ask for either verdict without producing any rows, and turn the warnings off with warnings_disabled() while keeping the checks. Three base classes carry this machinery: CheckedModel holds pydantic's model_config that every model shares and the 3 phases. RowModel[R] adds from_row() and to_row() , and holds the library's single cast . Notetype is the exception that doesn't use from_row() and to_row() and adds its own from_rows() and to_rows() because it aggregates the fields and templates. ProtobufModel adds from_bytes() and to_bytes() .
docs.title: Checks and warnings

docs.text: Every method that serializes a model has one of three roles: Role Methods What it does Phase prepare() , check() , warn() changes or judges a model, and produces nothing Emitter _row() , _bytes() , CardData._json() , Collection._sqlite() , _PackageBase._write_*() produces output, and calls only other emitters Entry point to_row() , to_rows() , to_bytes() , to_json() , write_sqlite() , write_apkg() , write_colpkg() runs the phases over its own tree, then its emitter A parent reaches its children through their emitters, never through their entry points. So a write judges each model once, from the entry point the caller invoked, however deep the model sits. The whole tree is prepared before anything is checked, because a parent's checks read its children. Otherwise a collection would refuse a card for an original deck that the card's own repair is about to clear. Notetype.to_row() runs only its row-local checks, so that to_rows() stays the point where a notetype is checked as a whole.
docs.title: Phases, emitters and entry points

docs.text: The checks have to run when a package is written, not only when a model is built. A model can change after its validators last ran: a list edited in place, such as notetype.templates.pop() , fires no validator. And a check that reads several objects, such as a card's template ordinal against its notetype's templates, can only be judged once all of them are in their final state. Pydantic validators cannot be made to run at that point. They run when a model is built and, with validate_assignment , when a field is assigned. Serializing a model runs no validator. The only way to make pydantic validate an existing model again is the revalidate_instances setting, which applies when a model is passed into a field of another model. It does not fit either way: With "never" , the default, the model is accepted as it is and nothing runs. With "always" , pydantic validates the model by building a new copy of it, and of every model it holds. A notetype shared by many notes would become one copy per note. An edit to the notetype in collection.notetypes would then no longer reach the notes, and the walk would judge every copy separately. So prepare() , check() and warn() are plain methods, and the entry points call them.
docs.title: Why the phases are methods and not pydantic validators

docs.text: The emitters change nothing. A write changes the models only in prepare() , in three places: TimestampedRowModel.prepare() sets the modification time of a note or notetype changed since it was last stamped. Collection.prepare() appends referenced objects to the collection's lists (see Referenced objects and the collection's lists ). Card.prepare() clears an original deck and due that the card's own deck no longer explains. Its validator makes the same repair, but a card cannot tell when its filtered deck turns normal. Each is idempotent: a second write with no edit in between writes the same rows. A model holds two kinds of state about the files around it, and only one of them follows a write: What the model was read from stays as the read left it: the fingerprint of the row, the modification time and id read, and a package's kept media source. Checks and warnings compare against it to report what changed since the read. What has been published follows the writes: the time a note or notetype was last stamped with, and the content it was stamped for. A later write compares against it, so an edit made after one write is stamped again by the next. A write that leaves the time where it was, in the same second as the last stamp or inside timestamping_disabled() , leaves this state too, and the next write stamps the edit. The published state lives on the model, not on the package or collection that wrote it. Anki compares an incoming note with the copy in the user's collection, and every package of a deck feeds that one collection, so a note written into two packages has one history. The second package carries the first one's stamp when the note is unchanged since, and a later one when it is not. A package written over its kept source is refused rather than followed for the same reason: the source is read state, describing the file the media is copied from (see A kept media source is checked before writing ).
docs.title: What a write changes on the model

docs.text: A phase called with recursive=True runs on every model reachable from where it is called, each object once. The walk lives in CheckedModel . It follows every CheckedModel that a field holds, directly or inside a container, so a field added later is covered without a hand-written branch. To keep the walk cheap, it reads only the fields whose annotation could hold a model, decided once per class. The strings in Note.fields and the scalar columns are never walked. A test checks that reading every field would reach the same objects. The walk gathers the reachable models breadth first, telling objects apart by identity, and runs the phase on each with recursive=False . An override reads recursive=False as "apply only my own rules". The result: A check from a note covers its notetype. A check from a review covers its card, the card's note and decks, and the notetype. From a collection, a notetype that every note shares is judged and warned about once, not once per note. Some details follow from how the walk is built: The set of models already seen lives for one call. A phase run inside another, such as a to_bytes() inside a check, starts a walk of its own. A model is handed to the phase before its fields are read, so the walk follows what the phase leaves behind. A collection inside a package collects its references when it is prepared, and the models it collects are then prepared too. An equal copy of a model held somewhere else is a separate object, and is judged separately. collect_* refuses an unequal one at write time.
docs.title: Walking the model tree

docs.text: checks_disabled() and warnings_disabled() turn off what a write runs automatically, so that a package Anki wrote can be written back even when it holds a value a genanki2 check rejects. checks_enabled() and warnings_enabled() turn them back on inside such a block (see Checks ). The switches are read at the entry point, never inside a phase, so an explicit check() or warn() inside the block still runs. Preparation runs whatever the switches say, since collecting fills the lists the writer writes from. Only the context managers are public, so a disabled state cannot outlive the block that set it. dbcheck_repairs_disabled() is the exception: its repairs run during validation, so the validators read it. See Switching the opt-out repairs off .
docs.title: Switching checks and warnings off

docs.text: Models refer to each other as objects: a card holds its note and its deck, a note holds its notetype, etc. The collection also keeps flat lists ( notes , decks , etc.) and the writer writes rows from those lists only. Two things can go wrong between the references and the lists: An object is referenced but missing from its list. Its row would not be written, and the row referring to it would name an id that the file does not hold. Two different objects share one id. For example, a card's note and a note already in collection.notes have the same id but different fields or modification times. Only one row can be written for that id, and nothing says which one. Collecting handles both ( Collection.collect_references() , which the prepare phase of every write runs). It appends each referenced object that is missing from its list, and raises when the list already holds a different object under the same id. Collecting compares content, because it decides which object gets written. So a caller can append just the cards it builds: their notes, decks, notetypes and presets fill in by themselves. Collection.check_referential_integrity() asks a narrower question: does every note's notetype, every card's note and every card's deck have its id in the matching list? It compares ids only, because the file stores only ids, and Anki resolves a row whose id is in the file whatever the object behind it holds. A note held in two different versions therefore passes this check, and only collecting refuses it. In a write, collecting runs before any check, so the check finds the lists already filled. Calling Collection.check() without preparing first reports a reference that collecting would have added.
docs.title: Referenced objects and the collection's lists

docs.text: A field or template row holds two values that the field or template does not own: the id of its notetype ( ntid ) and its position in the notetype's list ( ord ). So Field.to_row(notetype_id, ordinal) and Template.to_row(notetype_id, ordinal) take them as two plain ints and write them unchecked. The fields and templates tables declare no foreign key, so a wrong ntid would write rows that no notetype owns, without any error from SQLite. Every other value a write produces is checked: a model attribute by its annotation, and a row read with from_row() by model_validate . The two ints need no check of their own, because both come from the notetype. Notetype.to_rows() passes self.id , which Notetype already validates, and an ordinal from enumerate , which is 0, 1, 2… by construction. Validating the notetype's id covers the ntid of every row. What no validation can show is that to_rows() passes these values down correctly. Two tests check it: test_the_owning_id_comes_from_the_notetype changes the notetype's id and checks that every field and template row carries the new one. test_ordinals_follow_list_position reverses the list and checks that the ord values still run 0, 1, 2… in the new order. Checking the arguments as well would mean pydantic.validate_call on both methods. In lax mode it also turns "1" into 1 , so it would catch almost nothing the notetype does not already catch.
docs.title: Arguments of Field.to_row() and Template.to_row()

docs.text: How Anki reads a column decides what genanki2 does with a value out of range: Anki reads the column strictly: a value that does not fit makes the whole row unreadable, so the bound raises. A bound that raises refuses nothing Anki would open. Anki falls back to another value: Anki reads the fallback in place of what is stored, so every code path that loads the row sees the fallback, and an apkg import stores it. genanki2 repairs the value to the same fallback as it reads it, as a mandatory repair (see The repairs ). This covers the preset values under Bounded , Card.due and Card.original_due ( 0 outside the 32-bit signed range), and Review.time_ms ( 0 outside the 32-bit unsigned range). A value inside Anki's type can still be one that Anki's database check changes: a Card.template_ord above 30,000, or a Card.interval_days or Review.time_ms above 2**31 - 1 . Anki opens such a value as it is, so it is not a bound but an opt-out repair . Ids and times are bounded to values that make sense, even though Anki reads them as any 64-bit integer: an id is positive, and a time is 0 or later. Anki never writes anything else, and nothing in Anki gives a negative time or id a meaning. The cost is that genanki2 cannot read a collection holding such a value, so the bound is widened if one turns up in real data. Review.review_type is the one value read with a fallback that genanki2 keeps. Anki reads a review kind it does not know as a learning review, while the field is ReviewType | int and keeps the number. The fallback is what an older Anki makes of a kind a newer Anki added, and repairing it would erase the kind for the newer Anki too. usn is bounded only by its type, although Anki writes nothing below -1. A value below -1 makes an object count as already synced: a client sync sends the objects whose usn is -1, and the server those at or above the client's last count. Nothing genanki2 writes is held back by it, but only because of two Anki behaviours: an apkg import replaces every usn with the collection's own, and a colpkg restore forces a full sync, which uploads the whole file whatever each row's usn . If either changes, a value below -1 could keep an object from ever syncing, and the bound has to be reconsidered.
docs.title: Bounds that raise and bounds that repair
